Fifteen days, mapped: the coverage, who acted, and the documented ties

Top right, each dot is one piece on the story. Below it, each row is one actor and each chip one dated act. At left, each line is a documented tie between an actor and a company, a funder or a group: a contribution, a post held, a grant, an official act. Both slices repeat the same companies, funders and people at their left; a dashed box names an actor whose own row is in another slice. The ties are mapped outward from Anthropic and Open Philanthropy; Nvidia's are added where the same kind of record was searched (the note at the foot lists them), and each group's heading gives the rule for who is drawn. The figure sets these records side by side; it does not say one caused another.

THREE NEWSPAPERS
Background: The New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times cover chips and China.
No document here shows who their confidential intelligence sources are. Singapore's ministry denied the Journal's Oct 30 account in a statement timed the same day.
BYLINES WITH A TIE ON RECORD
No document here shows whether a tie shaped any of the five pieces. All 888 names in the bylines of the saved pages were looked up; five have a tie on record (three of them to the Tarbell Center). A reporter or columnist without one is not drawn, however often quoted.
ANALYSTS QUOTED OR POSTING
Background: Chris McGuire, now at the Council on Foreign Relations, "crafted and implemented" the Biden administration's chip export controls at the NSC, his biography says. CNAS published on chip smuggling in 2025.
No document here shows who, if anyone, prompted the posts or quotes. Drawn: 16 of the 282 analysts, experts and research groups quoted: those with a tie on record to Anthropic, Open Philanthropy or Nvidia, their own or through the organisation where they hold a post.
SENATE
Background: Democrats sen. Schumer was an original cosponsor of the GAIN AI Act on chip exports.
No document here shows any contact between a senator and the reporters or their sources.
HOUSE
Background: Rep. Mast's AI OVERWATCH Act, which would let Congress block advanced chip exports, passed his committee in January.
No document here shows whether anyone outside Congress had a hand in the Nov 4 letter.
The New York Times what it reported, from its own pages unless a chip says otherwise
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined
U.S. intelligence surveilled Alice Huang; its first report says that "Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings" and "chose not to do anything with the information", and that the Commerce Department's investigation of Megaspeed "was handed over this year to the Justice Department". Of Huang it says that when the president was first briefed "U.S. officials did not believe the Nvidia executive knew that Ms. Huang was gathering information for the Chinese", that "It is unclear whether intelligence officials have since updated their assessment", and that "some senior officials inside the Trump administration doubt that Mr. Huang could have remained unaware" of the role they had concluded she had. It dates that investigation to "late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data center in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious", the Nvidia equipment "still packed in boxes"; and says that Singapore "has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed" and that in 2025 its authorities "brought Ms. Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her". It recalls photographs "posted to LinkedIn" in June 2024, "just weeks before Megaspeed began its purchases", that "showed Mr. Huang alongside Ms. Huang at a bar in Taipei following a local technology trade show", and that in May 2025 "they were seen together again, leaving a restaurant in Taipei after a business dinner with other A.I. suppliers"; "Those details were described in a Times article last October", it says (the company's explanations of the photographs are on its chips of Oct 31 and Nov 9)
Reports, in its article on the chairmen's letter, that Sen. Warren "renewed her call for testimony" the week before, after its first report; Huang had turned down her request in June to appear before the Senate
A memo says China's spy agency recruited her
Reports that the Commerce Department "has approved dozens of Chinese companies to handle Nvidia's H200 chips, some of which have ties to firms under sanctions over national security". It says the administration "approved this Chinese firm to assemble Nvidia's advanced chips into the computers that create artificial intelligence", though its listed address "stands empty" and "there is little evidence the firm actually exists"; its owners have ties to a "Chinese private equity fund that the U.S. government placed on a trade blacklist in 2024", and two analysts "said they believed New Matrix may be a front for firms associated with that fund"; it "is the second Chinese company approved to handle Nvidia's H200 chips that does not seem to have any physical presence at its listed address". It adds that "several other Chinese companies approved to purchase H200 chips or assemble them into servers have ties to firms that have been blacklisted by the U.S. government, or that work as military contractors in China", and that the department "appears to have approved roughly two dozen Chinese firms to buy or handle" the chips. The paper also says that "Nvidia is now selling only small amounts of H200 chips to China" and that the firms "have not yet met that quota". The saved copy of the Times's page was updated on Nov 8; the Jerusalem Post relays these findings on Nov 7. The replies of the export bureau and of Nvidia are their chips of that day. Recalls, in its report on licences for chip sales to Chinese firms, what Nvidia disclosed for its summer quarter: "In the quarter that ended in July, H200 shipments to customers based in China made up less than 1 percent of Nvidia's revenue from data centers", and "The company also said in August that it was not assuming any sales to China in its estimate for data center revenue for the current quarter". The saved copy of the Times's page was updated on Nov 8; the Jerusalem Post relays both sentences on Nov 7, as "Nvidia's financial disclosures cited by NYT". Unite.AI, on Nov 5, in an article that does not mention the affair, had described the quarterly report for the period that ended July 26 in like terms: licences from February 2026 "allowed small amounts of H200 products to be shipped to specific China-based customers", the shipments made "represented less than 1% of Data Center revenue in the quarter covered by the report", the company "assessed that it was effectively foreclosed from competing in China's data-center computing market" without approval from both governments, and it "had been unable to pass any of the tariff to customers". A wire sentence words the disclosure: "Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Beijing government". It stands in RTÉ's page, first published on the evening of Nov 8 and updated on Nov 9; no first-day version of that page is saved, so the sentence may be newer than Nov 8 (a copy of the same article timed the next morning lacks it), and the Associated Press's dispatch of Nov 9 has it but for one word. The filing itself is saved, the company's quarterly report for the period that ended July 26: licences "would allow us to ship small amounts of H200 products to specific China-based customers, but such sales were restricted by the PRC government", and "Those shipments account for less than 1% of Data Center revenue in our most recent quarter"
Rubio oversaw the memo. Its report: the secretary of state "oversaw the drafting of the highly classified memo this past spring warning top Trump administration officials" of Huang's relationship, according to "multiple people briefed on the matter", and the memo "was circulated to administration officials with high-level security clearances ahead of a trip Mr. Trump took to China in May". Reports that Nvidia opened its inquiry after Huang "acknowledged to the company's board that he had been intimate with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined to be a Chinese spy" (as Boston.com carries the article)
Reports that a Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed "came to a sudden halt late last year" and was "transferred to the Justice Department", after Nvidia's general counsel emailed the investigators in August 2025. It says the transfer was "to avoid any potential compromise" of the investigation, that Justice "is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed", and that "it is not clear if other factors contributed". After the email, it says, Commerce officials "rapidly disclosed it to partner law enforcement agencies", and "The Justice Department requested that the Commerce Department pause its work on the investigation, and Commerce complied, one person familiar with the case said"; the outcome, it adds, "was a source of frustration to agents investigating Megaspeed, who had spent months building a case". Of the email it reports, from people familiar with the incident and a Commerce official: he told the agents the under secretary had given him permission to reach out about the case; Nvidia had asked them directly for a meeting with one of them, and when they turned it down he replied that he was unsure what the issue was, because the under secretary had said Nvidia could communicate with the bureau's employees. It adds that the investigators forwarded the email chain to the under secretary, and that since the president's return to office he and other leaders of the department "had mandated that any investigations into Nvidia and other outreach to the company first receive their approval"
Reports that the president was told aboard Air Force One in May, by Rubio, of the intelligence on Huang, which "contradicts the president's assertion" that he had not known then; the White House "disputed the reporting", it says, "without elaborating". Reports, in a profile of Alice Huang, that in 2024 "Taiwanese authorities began to monitor Ms. Huang's trips to the island at the suggestion of the U.S. government", citing a person familiar with the matter (as Business Standard carries the article). The profile also reports that Megaspeed "was named a Nvidia cloud partner" four days after a change of its ownership (the Journal's profile of the day before dates the partnership by a letter of November 2023: the Journal's act of Nov 9), and repeats, from the Times's first report (its act of Oct 29), that in late 2024 the Commerce Department "sent an official to inspect a Megaspeed data center", where "Some Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes". It also reports, from a person familiar with the investigation, that Singapore "prohibited Ms. Huang from leaving the country and brought her in for questioning in 2025 as part of an investigation into false declaration of imports", and that "There was insufficient evidence to suggest that Ms. Huang was complicit in the false declarations and investigations against her were concluded" (Singapore's own statement followed on Nov 12)
A second relationship, with a subordinate. Reports that Bessent "confronted" Lutnick at the White House over Megaspeed, as "described by people briefed on it"; a Commerce spokeswoman denies the conversation took place; it adds that the move to blacklist Megaspeed had earlier come before a meeting of cabinet deputies, where a Commerce under secretary "deferred on taking action, saying that the decision was up to Mr. Lutnick"
Recalls, in a profile of the interim chief (as the San Francisco Examiner carries it), that as chief financial officer she "expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict Nvidia sales to China": "In 2023, she said on a call with financial analysts that China accounted for 20% to 25% of the company's data center revenue"
The Wall Street Journal what it reported, from its own page saved by hand and from copies its licensed partners carry
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined
Reports that officials in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan "have grown concerned" that an executive close to Huang "is a Chinese intelligence source", citing people familiar with the matter (Singapore denied the account in a statement timed the same day). It says authorities in Singapore and Taiwan "had separately investigated Alice Huang's ties to China, at one point putting physical surveillance teams on her", and that a Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed, begun in late 2024, "largely stalled", with the Justice Department "now leading the probe". It quotes Megaspeed's statement of late 2025 that reviews "confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities", and recalls the arrest in March of a co-founder of the server maker Super Micro "on charges of violating U.S. export-control laws"; Super Micro, it adds, said then that it was cooperating with investigators and Nvidia that "compliance with export restrictions is a top priority"; both companies "denied wrongdoing at the time", and he pleaded not guilty
Reports, in an article on who could succeed Huang, that Nvidia's latest proxy statement warns it is "highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team" and that a failure to ensure effective succession planning could "hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success". Reports, in a profile of Alice Huang (as To Vima and a licensed Dow Jones copy carry the article), that "According to a November 2023 letter posted on its website, Megaspeed became a member of an Nvidia partnership program, a status that typically grants priority access to the latest chips". Its editorial board writes the same day that Megaspeed "was then sold to a Singapore-based shell company in November 2023", and that Nvidia made it a cloud partner "Soon afterward". The Times's profile of the next day puts the designation four days after the change of ownership (the Times's act of Nov 10)
Reports that the board "is preparing to oust" Huang and "to meet as soon as today to determine his future", citing people familiar with the matter. Reports, in a Heard on the Street column that evening, that Nvidia stopped reporting revenue tied to Singapore, 22% of its revenue until then, in the quarter after it blocked Megaspeed: from the quarter that ended in October 2025 it reported revenue by "the location of the customers' headquarters" and no longer by "customer billing location". "It isn't clear if the two are related", the column says. It quotes the filing: the change "provides a better representation of the geographic profile of our revenue", since billing locations "often reflected a customer's centralized invoicing location, even though our products were almost always shipped elsewhere"; and the filing of a quarter before: "customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere"
Financial Times what it reported, from its own page
Its report of Sep 4, 2025 that Anthropic would stop selling AI services to groups majority-owned by Chinese entities cited "an Anthropic executive familiar with the matter", as Bloomberg Law relays it. No record here shows who the sources of its Nov 6 report were
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined
Reports that the U.S. government "believes" Huang "had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China's main intelligence agency", citing people familiar with the matter. It says a memo by U.S. officials stating this "was shared with a small group of top US officials shortly before" the president flew to Beijing; that sentence stands in a copy of the page updated on Nov 7, and the report's earlier saved forms (an archived opening and its reporter's post of Nov 6) do not reach it, so it may be newer than the report's first day. The first saved page that has the president himself notified is a relay of the next day (the FT's row, Nov 7). Its reporter's post of the report: 3.4M views. Reports that before the president's trip to China in May, when he learnt that Huang was not in the group, he called him, and Huang flew to Alaska, where he boarded the presidential jet during a stopover
Engadget, relaying the FT's report of the day before, writes that the president, "along with select American officials, were notified about it before his trip to Beijing earlier this year", and that he "reportedly took no action about that information". It is the first saved page that has the president himself notified; the saved copy of the FT's own report says the memo went to "a small group of top US officials" (its act of Nov 6), and the FT writes on Nov 9 that it had reported the president was briefed (its act of Nov 9)
Writes, in its report of the president's remarks that day, that it "previously reported that the president was briefed in May on a top-secret memo that included information about the affair"; its report of Nov 6, as saved, says the memo "was shared with a small group of top US officials shortly before" his flight to Beijing. In the same sentence it has the president saying he "had been informed about Huang's situation only recently", and it prints his reply when asked about the memo: "I'd certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned" (his act of that day). The Times reports a briefing aboard the plane the next day (the Times's act of Nov 10). Reports, from "two investors pitched on the deal", that in early 2025 an executive of Megaspeed and her business partner sought investment for a "south-east Asia data centre project worth several hundred million dollars": the pair "said they had" what one investor quotes as "no problem securing GPUs" and "cited Alibaba as a client of the project, according to one investor present". It adds that she "did not disclose any close relationship with Nvidia's chief executive" in the pitch; that "The allegation of espionage could not be independently verified by the FT"; that of the photographs of the two "None of the photos suggest inappropriate relationships and several are in a group setting"; that Megaspeed has "strongly denied allegations of any illicit activity involving chips"; and, from company documents, that Alibaba, through a Singaporean subsidiary, lent money to a Malaysian subsidiary of Megaspeed in June 2024. It says neither the executive nor her partner could be reached, and that Alibaba "did not immediately respond to a request for comment"
Reports that the Commerce Department "sought over the past two months to delay new inclusions" on the entity list ("one of the people said"), its officials saying they needed more information about some companies; the paper adds: "It was unclear if Megaspeed was one of the companies, but the delay has meant it remains off the entity list". It reports, from people familiar with the matter, that the state, energy and Treasury departments and the Pentagon "were among the agencies that were pushing for Megaspeed's inclusion on the list". Reports, in its piece "Too big to fire", that Megaspeed, according to that company's documents, "has been the recipient of loans from the US chip group in 2024"

Publishes "Jensen Huang should resign": "An investigation is necessary to see just how bad the incident was", but "its findings are not needed to decide what to do with Jensen, who in recent weeks appears to have misled his own employees, investors and the public"; "even if Alice Huang is an ordinary civilian, the affair and events surrounding it are unacceptable for a CEO of a major company"; "in recent weeks Nvidia and Huang have issued multiple statements we now know to be false". "In the worst case, Nvidia may have fundamentally undermined American national security and AI leadership"; "we do not know if the affair was disclosed to Nvidia's board or if Huang removed himself from decision-making involving Megaspeed"; it does not know whether the company's spokesman knew his statements were false ("if not, Huang appears to have misled his own executives as well"); "Nvidia's board may keep him around"
In a post that a newsletter of Nov 10 quotes: the company's spokesman "has put out multiple statements in recent weeks that we now know are false. Unclear, of course, if he believed them to be true at the time"; "Jensen himself directly lied to Bloomberg's" reporters
Zvi Mowshowitz author of a newsletter on AI
The Survival and Flourishing Fund lists a $200,000 "unconditional gift" to him in 2024 from Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic's first funding round in 2021; he has written of serving as a recommender for that fund. No record here ties the gift to this piece
In his weekly newsletter, on the Times report: "you should be entirely unshocked that such a spy is out there"; "this is me not updating"; and he goes on: "Nor am I updating on the rest of the story, about how Nvidia has managed to compromise the White House, largely through flattery, and how when the White House noticed a Chinese spy it did not announce this fact"
Publishes "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Had an Affair With a Chinese Spy": "National security has been compromised. He must resign"; "I would be very surprised if Jensen Huang knew he was being compromised by a Chinese agent"; he accepts as "a mitigating factor" that Huang "was up against actual professional spies and an active operation to compromise him"; "If he will not resign, the board must remove him. If the board will not remove him, the United States Government should force him to step down"; and anyone in the government "who knowingly let this go on for a year should be offering their resignation as well". He also writes that the affair "is not necessary to explain" Huang's conduct on chip sales to China: "He might or might not have done that anyway, or done that to the same extent"
In his weekly newsletter, "Spy Versus Guy": removing Huang "will be tricky because Jensen Huang deliberately tried to make himself unfireable, with over 50 direct reports and no succession plan"
Jordan Schneider founder of ChinaTalk

An episode of his podcast, with him among the speakers, lists a part titled "Jensen, spies, and the J-5 firing". The recording was not heard
His podcast releases two episodes: an "emergency pod", "Jensen and His Spy", with Chris McGuire, and one recorded, it says, "Friday afternoon, before the FT reported", with a part on "the alleged spy in Jensen Huang's orbit". The recordings were not heard
Publishes "The Spy Who Leased Me", the newsletter page of his podcast with Chris McGuire on the affair, which his feed dates the day before

Tells CNBC what Democrats are likely to probe: CNBC has him say that one question is "whether the Trump administration was aware of Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy, and whether the Nvidia CEO influenced American policy", and quotes him: "That is going to be very high up on the Democrats' lists of people to investigate to try to figure out to what extent was the Trump administration aware of what was going on". Ryan Fedasiuk Foundation for American Innovation
CSET at Georgetown: listed as research analyst, 2019–22 rosters
Open Philanthropy made three awards to his institution, the Foundation for American Innovation: $976,000 for AI policy in 2023–24 (the second an exit grant) and $2.7M for energy permitting in 2026. No record here ties an award to him
Tells the Journal: "It was this unparalleled access to politicos and other industry titans that made him such an attractive target for Chinese intelligence to begin with"
A podcast episode titled "Jensen Huang Must Resign" is released. The day is the release time in the data of a summary page that prints no date; the recording was not heard. The page's summary has him say that whether sensitive information reached Chinese intelligence is unknown ("we really don't know anything about" the nature of the relationship), and of the motive he alleges: "I'm reading between the lines"
Tells Scientific American Huang is in "almost every aspect of the company"; writes at his institute's site that it is "a sad day for Nvidia", that "there is reason to be optimistic" about the company and that stepping down "was dignified, and ultimately the right decision". Also to Scientific American: "The longer this drags on", "the more distracted the company will grow"; and "I don't think it's right to conceive of this as 'if Jensen goes, then there goes a huge blow to the company's technical capability'". His piece ends: "gratitude does not excuse Huang's personal misconduct", nor should admiration for him or blame over the scandal "obscure deeper problems in his company's conduct". Tells the Washington Post, of accounts defending Huang: "There are many actors in the American economy who believe that Mr. Huang's personal status as CEO of the company is an essential part of American economic growth"
Chris McGuire Council on Foreign Relations
NSC technology office: deputy senior director, 2022–24
Tarun Chhabra: scheduled for the same session, Taipei, Jun 6, 2026
The Council on Foreign Relations lists Nvidia among its corporate members, in its Bronze tier, as of Sep 3, 2026
Recap post asks why Commerce took no action. 9.4M views
Post: "Jensen's behavior is only half the story"; "Obviously Nvidia needs to take significant steps in its operations, security, and policy advocacy to ensure it takes national security concerns more seriously". In the same post: "The biggest problem remains unaddressed"; "it is even more important that the Department of Commerce tighten up export controls to prevent things like this from ever happening again". Posts that Sunday: "So Rubio himself is worried about Jensen's romantic relationship with the Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive, meaning the intel was validated at the highest levels of government. But still, Commerce has done nothing to limit AI chip shipments to Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. Why?" (The National embeds the post in its report of Nov 9)
Tells Bloomberg, as The National relays it: "You have the CEO of one of the biggest companies in America, that is potentially compromised by the Chinese and they have some information on him - it really needs to be looked into"
Tells the FT, for its report on the delayed listing of Megaspeed: "It is mind-boggling that commerce knew months ago that Megaspeed is being run by a Chinese spy but did nothing to stop them from buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia chips"; "I can't come up with a single good reason for that inaction". The FT adds that he said the department "should take steps to prevent any untrusted companies such as Megaspeed from buying AI chips without an export licence, which he said was required under existing export-control rules"; guest on the ChinaTalk podcast. In a piece of the Council on Foreign Relations, where he is a fellow: Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention"; of rules that would require licences, "the Department of Commerce is refusing to enforce them"; it should "impose new controls that ban Chinese companies from renting remote access to the AI chips that they are currently prohibited from purchasing". Tells the Journal, of the chip-export bills: "They should just be pushed now and voted on, up or down, as a way to signal Congress's concern about this issue and how it's being handled". In a post that a newsletter of Nov 10 quotes: "Nvidia's most advanced chips remain available to Megaspeed"; "And for some reason, @BISgov refuses to cut them off"; "the best evidence is the fact that the MSS is actively trying to convince us to loosen them!"
Tells the Washington Post by email that he had "definitely" noticed the accounts that targeted his posts, and had assumed they were Chinese bot accounts. The New York Post, as AOL carries it, has him call the Commerce Department's handling of the Megaspeed matter "stunning", and quotes him: "The president has been pretty clear - no Blackwells to China"; "And the way that Commerce is implementing export controls is massively undermining the president's policy". CBS News quotes him: "The real scandal here is the lack of enforcement of export controls"; it has him add that the department had known for as long as a year that Megaspeed was run by a woman the U.S. believes to be a Chinese spy, "and they did nothing"; and: "Either Lutnick doesn't know how to do his job or he is protecting Huang". CBS says the department "did not respond to a request for comment". The saved copy of CBS's page was changed on Nov 13; ANI carries the first sentence that evening, U.S. Eastern time, and no saved page of Nov 12 carries the last
Erich Grunewald Institute for AI Policy and Strategy
Institute for AI Policy and Strategy: senior researcher
Co-author of the 2025 CNAS report on AI chip smuggling
CNAS, which published that report, lists Nvidia among its supporters for Oct 2024 to Sep 2025, in its $50,000 to $99,999 band
Tells Al Jazeera he thinks recent events likely "add momentum" to chip bills
In an article of his own on The Substrate: "Together, smuggling and remote access probably account for almost half of the compute China has access to, more than its own AI chip industry has produced"; he calls the estimates he uses "highly uncertain" and says that varying one of them "moves the combined share between about 36% and 61%". Of the company: "NVIDIA has done more to stop smuggling in 2026", "But one might fairly ask why NVIDIA didn't do this in 2024 or 2025, when there were already many credible reports of smuggling and NVIDIA was saying there was no evidence of it". Of the board's inquiry: "It remains to be seen how impartial and thorough that investigation will be". Of the department: "Nor do we know why the Commerce Department didn't stop AI chip sales to Megaspeed when it may have known that one of the company's senior executives was suspected of being a Chinese spy". And of the controls: "the export controls are working, but that they're not as effective as they could be". The article also repeats the report on OpenAI's chip of Nov 4: "OpenAI has reportedly avoided taking a public position on AI chip exports to China so as not to alienate NVIDIA, on whose chips it relies", with Nvidia's answer in brackets, not OpenAI's (Nvidia "allocates fairly" and customers "can choose whatever solution is best for them"); and it recalls that in May 2025 Nvidia accused Anthropic of telling "tall tales" about chip smuggling (the two companies' tie line). Fortune quotes him, in its account of Megaspeed's network in Singapore and Malaysia: "AI chip distributors and resellers often spend too little effort vetting customers, usually relying on paperwork the customer provides". Fortune's page was published late on Nov 11 and changed the next morning

Letter with Sen. Wyden opens a probe of chip-export approvals; it says the administration "did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat"; it asks the department to preserve all records of its tariff investigation of semiconductors, of Nvidia's export licence applications and of its communications with and about Nvidia and Huang. The letter calls the tariff collected on the chips "what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system", says the department approved sales to Chinese companies "with government and military ties", and says: "There appears to be a profound lack of due diligence in Commerce's process for approving these Chinese buyers of Nvidia chips". It says the president's approval of the H200 exports, "apparently granted with knowledge of Mr. Huang's compromised position and only after Mr. Huang and Nvidia directed at least $26 million toward President Trump's personal priorities such as the White House ballroom", "raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration"; that his use of the tariff statute "appears to have done the opposite, undermining U.S. national security and putting Americans at risk"; and the records it asks for include "the report you allegedly transmitted to the President on December 22, 2025"

THE ADMINISTRATION
Background: The government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip for sale to China this year. As CNBC relays the Times's reporting, policymakers received the intelligence memo last spring and Trump, once briefed, "chose not to do anything."
No document here shows who gave the intelligence to reporters. The reports cite "people briefed on intelligence surveillance."
NVIDIA
Background: The board had no chair, and the company had "not set out a clear succession plan," Fortune reported; Huang held about 3.6% of the stock.
No document here shows what the board's inquiry found; the saved accounts do not give its findings.
SHARE PRICES
Background: AMD and Broadcom compete with Nvidia for AI chip sales.

ANTHROPIC
Background: Backs "smart export controls on AI chips"; gave $40 million to Public First Action, for policy and education work, it says, not candidate elections; its PAC gave to candidates of both parties; has hired former administration officials.

Ordered agencies to stop using Anthropic, Feb 2026, with a six-month phase-out for agencies using it
Nvidia gave $25M to his ballroom project, HuffPost reports (the Times's first report gives a lower bound from one person: it "later donated at least $20 million to Mr. Trump's ballroom fund"); CNBC adds "$1 million to his 2025 inaugural fund"

Before the order of February 2026 on this pair's other line: Axios wrote on Oct 16, 2025 that Anthropic's chief executive "publicly supported Kamala Harris for president, and has been noticeably absent from White House tech events", "ceding that ground to rivals like OpenAI"; five days later he wrote of "Our alignment with the Trump administration on key areas of AI policy", that "I strongly agree with Vice President JD Vance's recent comments on AI", and that he had attended a summit in Pennsylvania with the president, "where he and I had a good conversation about US leadership in AI"
Gizmodo recalls, on the day of the first report: "In December, the Trump administration gave Nvidia the green light to sell its powerful H200 chips to Chinese buyers", in "a deal that guaranteed the government 25% of the profits". The Times's report of that day has Huang negotiating "a deal with Mr. Trump that allowed the U.S. government to take a 25 percent stake of certain Nvidia chips that the government allows to be sold to China". The Spectator, on Nov 12: in December 2025 the president "announced conditional permission for sales of H200, a different chip, to approved Chinese customers, with a proposed 25 percent government share"; it sets this after the briefing the Times reported
At his Halloween party, asked if he still has confidence in Huang as an adviser: "I would like to say yes. I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary"; says the matter is "very complex" and will be looked at "very closely"; asked about the intelligence concerns, in the pool report of that evening: "I didn't know about the specific thing, but I hope he's going to be okay"
Axios, as CNBC relays it: at the meeting where Bessent pressed Lutnick, with Cabinet officials backing the export controls, he says "Let's get it done"; Implicator, citing Axios too: he had signed off on such curbs three times. A Commerce spokeswoman tells CNBC Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation"; Implicator notes that the denial "did not address the three approvals or the Oval Office meeting". Axios's own page, saved as far as its opening, says he "on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year"; the words quoted from the meeting stand behind its sign-up prompt and are given from the relays
Asked "Should he stay on as CEO of Nvidia?", answers: "I think so. Oh, yes" (two published transcripts of that Sunday's gaggle). Asked "do you wish that you had acted on the intelligence when you were briefed about the spying last year?": "No, I don't think so. I think, you know, I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it". NBC's account: he thinks Huang "should remain CEO of Nvidia". Also that Sunday: "I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on" (FT); asked whether Huang would take part in the coming summit in China: "I don't know, but I'd certainly take him" (Al Jazeera); "I haven't heard he's done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else" (the Times)
Says Huang told him he "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy"; says "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape", and does not say what the something else is; "I hope there's no problem", and "If there is a problem, we'll let you know about it" (NBC). Asked whether he knew of the concerns when Huang flew with him to China in May: "No, I didn't hear about it then"; pressed on whether he had been briefed a year earlier: "I'd certainly check with the intelligence people. They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn't make much of an impact on me" (the Times). The Journal: he "declined to provide a detailed explanation of when he learned about the federal government's concerns". Says Huang will not accompany him to China the next week and that he does not plan to raise the matter with Xi (the Times). Rev's transcript of the press conference gives the question and the whole answer: "Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week?"; "No, I don't think so. I mean, maybe I'm sure President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man", and: "I feel very confident that he'll be in good shape" (the Times and CNBC print the answer that day). Of Huang's denial: "I really believe him" (FT); of when he learned of the concerns: "Not too long ago" (the Journal)
The Times reports, from two people briefed on the call, that he called Huang that Tuesday "and urged him to keep fighting for his job" (as Business Standard carries the article). NBC recalls that Huang had not been on the White House's first list for the trip to China, "according to reports at the time", and that the president denied it, "writing on social media on May 12 that Huang would be joining him on the state visit": "Jensen is currently on Air Force One"
Posts: "there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!". In a podcast interview released that day, asked whether Huang should have resigned ("Should he have stepped down?" in the transcript): "The big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don't know if that's been determined yet. But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different"; he goes on: "I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man", and: "I spoke to him yesterday. He's going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That's what he told me" (the call was on Wednesday). HuffPost reports that in an interview with a radio host that Thursday he "called the scandal a sad episode for Huang": "What a horrible thing that is! It's so sad to see that happen". Political.org, the same day, has him call the scandal "so sad to see happen" "hours after the company announced Huang had stepped down"
Secretary of State Rubio
Axios, as Gizmodo relays it: was at the Situation Room meeting and "on Bessent's side for a more strict approach to exports". Gizmodo adds that the administration denied to Axios and the Times that the confrontation took place
Asked whether Huang was cut out of government meetings or briefings: "I can't comment on any of that. I just can't comment because of the nature of it"; and then: he "can't comment on an internal corporate matter that's going on with Nvidia", and: "I don't know anything about that part of it". Asked again about Huang and how important a thorough investigation is: "I'm not going to comment on an internal corporate matter for them"; asked whether he sees a national security concern: "I'm just not going to comment on it"; of the travel to China: "you'll have to ask the White House", "I don't handle the - that part of our operation". Commerce Secretary Lutnick and his department
Axios, as Gizmodo relays it: the president told Lutnick "let's get it done"; Lutnick replied "I'll develop some options and come back" (Implicator, citing Axios too, dates these discussions to Nov 5). Gizmodo adds that the administration denied to Axios and the Times that the confrontation took place. Axios, as ZeroHedge relays it: asked by Bessent why Megaspeed is not on the entity list, Lutnick answers "I don't know. I'll look into it". In a second report of Axios, of an Oval Office meeting with the president that day, he warns that the controls "will start a trade war with China". In the Times's account of the first exchange he answers that Commerce "could now move quickly to put restrictions on Megaspeed in place". A Commerce spokeswoman: "This is false. Secretary Bessent and Secretary Lutnick had no such conversation". Implicator's account of the Axios report has him appear to agree at the first exchange and then mutter "I need to check with the president". CNN, on Nov 11, from people familiar with the matter: "Confronted on it by Bessent last Thursday, Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action"; by the same account "Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list"
A spokesman for its export bureau tells the Times, for its report on licences for chip sales to Chinese firms, that it carefully reviews all applications for national security risks; the agency says it imposed $324 million of penalties for export violations in 2025 and hired more than 90 officers this year. MadRobot recalls, in its account of the Times's report on the buyers the department approved, that Reuters "had reported that around 10 Chinese firms, among them Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and JD.com, were cleared" in May, "though no chips had been delivered at the time". Axios reports on Nov 10, as Raw Story relays it, that Reuters had reported on May 14 that the department "had approved roughly 10 Chinese companies to buy Nvidia's H200 chips", and that its secretary "received a sensitive warning about Nvidia's CEO before his agency signed off on chip sales tied to China"; "Some approvals came before the warning". The Seoul Economic Daily, on Nov 11, in an article it marks as translated by machine from Korean, dates the approvals themselves to May 14
After the Times reports on Monday morning that its investigation of Megaspeed ran "until August 2025, when the probe was abruptly transferred to the Department of Justice following outreach from Nvidia's general counsel" (CNBC's summary), a spokesman for its export-control bureau tells CNBC: "BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book", and: "BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling, and enforcement is at an all-time high". Bloomberg's report of that afternoon that the general counsel "intervened in a US government probe" prints the same two sentences from "a spokesperson for the agency". A department spokesman tells the Times it "had been aggressively enforcing its rules"; an official tells the paper the under secretary told the agents to "continue to handle the case strictly by the book" and did not order them to give Nvidia information. Extends to Jan. 10, 2027 its pause on a rule that would stretch entity-list limits to companies majority-owned by listed firms. The rule that does so is in the Federal Register of Monday, Nov 9, and takes effect that day: "The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027"; the Register notes that it was filed on Nov 5 at 4:15 pm. Yahoo Finance, on Nov 10, says the department did so "On Monday"; Implicator dates it Nov 5. Bloomberg reports that its export bureau "has declined to impose restrictions on Nvidia's ability to do business with the firm despite calls for such a step from senior levels of the Trump administration" (the firm is Megaspeed; the report gives no day). By the same report, late in 2025 the Justice Department "requested that BIS pause its efforts, the people said", and "BIS has not made any progress since then, despite the agency having enough evidence to move forward". The bureau's statement in the report is on its other chip of that day. The Information reports, as its reporter posts on the evening of Nov 9: "There have been renewed pushes in recent weeks within the Commerce Department for rule-making on both the remote access loophole and controls around lithography tooling", "though current and former Commerce officials are skeptical the efforts will advance". The post says the White House's feedback to Congress (its chip of that day) would force the department "to take action on an issue it has dragged its feet on", and that export-control policy could pass Congress "even as the Commerce Department remains paralyzed". Semafor links the report the next day: the department "has reportedly begun readying a new set of semiconductor export controls". The later report that it is finalizing a rule is on its chip of Nov 11
Tells the FT it does not comment on internal discussions about the entity list; the department says it has "enforced aggressively across the board, including on smuggling advanced chips" and cites six investigations with "criminal charges against 17 defendants". Politico reports, as WinBuzzer relays it that day, that staff of its export bureau "had warned about the risk of Nvidia chips being diverted to China in dozens of reports, without prompting meaningful action"; a bureau spokesperson said it "enforces the rules by the book and that chip-smuggling enforcement is at a record high". The Bulwark relays the Politico report on Nov 11. CNN, on Nov 11, as a local station carries it: senior officials, the secretary among them, "were briefed months ago about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang"
Axios, as Implicator and CryptoNews relay it: beside her denial of the confrontation, the department's spokeswoman "would not immediately comment on the other allegations". The allegation, as Implicator gives Axios's report: the secretary "has held up chip export curbs President Trump approved three times this year"; Implicator adds that Commerce "says it uses the blacklist every day against bad actors". Axios's own page, saved as far as its opening, says one official "has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick". By Implicator's account of the same report, the secretary and a Commerce under secretary "resisted pressure to proceed"; the under secretary "had also received repeated warnings about Megaspeed in deputy-level meetings", and said: "That's a decision for the secretary"; "He's stalling it out", one official said of the secretary (the Times's account of the deferral is on its chip of that day). The Information reports on Wednesday, Nov 11, as Investing.com relays it at 11:22 that night, Eastern, that the department "is preparing to finalize a rule that will prevent Chinese artificial intelligence companies from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through data centers located in other countries", "citing two people familiar with the matter": "The rule could be announced this month", and "The expanded controls will apply to seven additional countries, including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand". CNBC relays the report the next morning: the department "is finalizing a rule aimed at preventing Chinese AI firms from remotely accessing advanced chips through data centers in other countries". MLQ.ai, in an article it says its AI newsroom produced, adds on Nov 12 that "Commerce is still consulting other agencies before the rule can be finalized". SBS, in a page it says was translated by AI, gives more of the report on Nov 12: the seven countries are "Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, Norway, and South Africa"; they "will need to obtain export licenses to bring in Nvidia Blackwell-class or superior chips", while "data centers operated by U.S. companies in these countries will be exempt from licensing on the condition that they restrict remote access from arms-embargoed nations such as China and Russia", and "must report their local customers and computing scale", while the seven countries "will also be required to notify the Department of Commerce of the recipients and intended uses of the chips, and be subject to ongoing monitoring"; by the same account the department "also plans to officially scrap" the Biden-era AI diffusion rule, a repeal the administration announced "last May" and for which it "had not completed the formal procedures". An earlier report of The Information, on renewed pushes in the department for such a rule, is on its chip of Nov 9. Tells the Times, beside its denial of the confrontation, that the decision whether to add companies to the entity list "was an administration-wide one". The New Republic recalls what its secretary said in July 2025 of Nvidia's sales to China: "We don't sell them our best stuff, not our second-best stuff, not even our third-best. The fourth one down, we want to keep China using it". The Wire China reports that a spokesperson for its export bureau "declined to comment when asked if it is considering taking any measures targeting Megaspeed". The page was first published on Nov 11 and changed on Nov 13; the passage may be newer than its first day. Its export bureau answers Rep. Huizenga's charge, made in an interview with Politico that Wednesday, that the bureau has "been less responsive than they should be" to lawmakers' requests for briefings on the matter. A spokesperson tells Politico: "BIS has a strong relationship with Members of Congress from both parties on our committees of jurisdiction. And we engage with them frequently", and: "The details of scheduling are best left to our respective office staff". Politico reports, from two people close to the process, that its Bureau of Industry and Security "is one of several parts of the administration currently negotiating with the Hill on three proposals to tighten chip restrictions lawmakers have proposed including in the annual defense authorization bill". The page gives the talks no day
A spokeswoman tells CNBC Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation". The Internet Governance Project's timeline says that in its investigation of Megaspeed, from late 2024 to mid 2025, its export bureau "conducted on-site inspections and supply chain audits across Southeast Asian data centers to verify serial numbers and end-user declarations". MS NOW recalls, in its report of that day, that the department "greenlit" Megaspeed "as a buyer of Nvidia's advanced chips earlier this year"; the page gives no detail of the approval. A spokeswoman tells NBC News, as Just the News relays it that evening: "Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions". Just the News writes that he "has reportedly agreed Thursday to testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee next month"; Sen. Scott's letter of that day had asked for him on Dec. 10 (Scott's act of Nov 12). Kharon reports that its Bureau of Industry and Security "declined to comment on the record", beside The Information's report that the department "is readying a proposed rule to add seven more countries" to its list of countries under AI-chip export restrictions, "to stop Chinese companies from accessing that compute power remotely". The page was first published on Nov 12 and changed on Nov 13; the passage may be newer than its first day. The New York Post, as AOL carries it, reports a former official's account that "bad findings about Megaspeed" circulated in the department "at least as far back as the summer of 2025", and recalls Bloomberg's report of the call from Nvidia's general counsel to its under secretary. A spokesperson for its export bureau, "When reached for comment", confirms that it is "actively considering new rules to address remote access with interagency partners", says "BIS has a strong track record of enforcement across the board, including in cases involving Nvidia and its products", calls any concerns that the under secretary's dealings with Nvidia were inappropriate "entirely unfounded", and adds that his "response to Nvidia was absolutely correct": "He handled the situation impartially and with integrity, as he always does". Semafor reports that the Nvidia fallout "fuels questions about Lutnick's staying power", and quotes a commentator it calls an ally of the Treasury secretary: "the working level at Treasury was all over Commerce about chip sales for over a year". A department spokesperson tells Semafor that "Treasury and Commerce have a great working relationship" and that both "are committed to advancing President Trump's agenda". ChosunBiz, in an article that starts from the Journal's report of that day on the pressure on the secretary, writes: "Responding to the controversy, Commerce said it sought only to maintain smooth ties with key U.S. companies and has no special private relationship". The page names neither whom the department answered nor the day; the Journal's own report has a Commerce official say that the secretary and Huang "don't have any kind of special relationship beyond the commerce secretary wanting a good rapport with one of the most important U.S. companies", and says that representatives of the department "didn't respond to requests for comment"; the pages do not show whether the two outlets give one answer. Politico reports, on the evening of Nov 12, that several people with knowledge of the department's operations question whether the under secretary who heads its export bureau "could reasonably shoulder the blame for decisions that ultimately rested with Lutnick, who they say maintained unusually tight control over his subordinates"; a former department official says of the under secretary: "He doesn't make any decisions without Lutnick's expressed written consent". In a statement, a spokesperson for the bureau says the two "have a strong working relationship, and both are honored to serve under President Trump to his vision to Make America Great Again". The page gives the practice no dates
Treasury Secretary Bessent
Axios, as the Daily Caller relays it: in a Situation Room meeting he asks Lutnick "How come Megaspeed isn't on the entities list?" The Times reports the exchange too, as "described by people briefed on it", and prints a Commerce spokeswoman's denial that the conversation took place. Axios's own page is saved as far as its opening, which has him confronting Lutnick "over a failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns"; the question quoted here stands behind its sign-up prompt and is given from the relay
The Treasury Department declines to comment to the FT for its report on the entity list
Trade Representative Greer
Axios, as CNBC relays it: was in the Situation Room when Bessent pressed Lutnick and, with other Cabinet officials, "supported the controls". A Commerce spokeswoman tells CNBC Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation"
Tells CNBC "Nvidia is a structurally important company", and: "The reality is the AI buildout, data centers, the next industrial revolution - that's happening"; of the scandal: "From time to time, you have scandal, or you have developments at companies with leadership, et cetera"; "And obviously, we remain concerned", he adds: "We want to make sure that when we're selling our chips to the world, we want the world to be on the AI stack, but we want the crown jewels to remain in U.S. hands or in the hands of our allies". Yonhap Infomax, in an English page it says was translated by AI, gives more of the interview: he calls the matter "extremely important to us" and says "national security is the most important issue to the President"; he puts the chance that the president raises it with China's president at the next week's summit as "small", saying: "Discussions about economic security and export controls are not something we negotiate with China. This is an internal matter". Finwire, a Swedish news agency that credits Reuters for its account of the interview, gives the same two answers. Semafor, in a piece on the trade truce with China, recalls that he said in September that negotiators had taken export controls "off the table" as a "national security issue"
White House spokespeople
With the CIA and the National Security Agency, declines to comment to the Times for its first report
With the CIA, declines to comment to the Times and to the FT for their reports of the memo. Punchbowl News reports that it "has offered feedback on two major export control bills under negotiation for the National Defense Authorization Act, according to multiple sources": officials "have offered technical assistance to the MATCH Act and the AI Overwatch Act", and "The feedback signals the White House isn't shutting them down and is engaging with Capitol Hill". The page gives the feedback no day. Asked how the administration handled the information: "These sources have no idea what they're talking about". The Information reports, as its reporter posts on the evening of Nov 9, that "In late October, the White House sent feedback to Congressional staff on two export control bills attached to the NDAA", and that "the feedback called for a provision attached to the Overwatch Act that would order Commerce to close the remote access loophole on chips covered by the bill"; the post credits another reporter, who "had this first". Punchbowl News had reported feedback on the same two bills on Nov 6 (its chip of that day); neither page shows that the two reports are of one communication. Declines to comment to the FT for its report on the entity list. For the Times's report that the president was told of the concerns on his trip to China, its press office declines to comment on the record and emails a statement on background that points to the president's remarks of Monday and disputes the reporting, "without elaborating". Asked by Newsweek whether the president would expand on his remarks, the press office refers it to his comments at Monday's briefing. CNN reports that the secretary of state "briefed President Donald Trump on intelligence that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a potential Chinese spy as they traveled to China in May aboard Air Force One", from "a source familiar with the matter"; the president had said on Monday that he learned of the concerns only recently. One of its officials, by CNN's account, "on Tuesday directed CNN to Trump's comments on Monday", adding: "These sources have no idea what they're talking about" (the sentence its spokesperson gave another outlet on Monday: its chip of that day)
After reports that the Commerce secretary "repeatedly blocked President Donald Trump's efforts to crack down on efforts to smuggle Nvidia chips into China" (CNBC's words), one of its officials says in a statement to CNBC that Thursday: "Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump's America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments", and the president "maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history". Semafor prints the same two sentences that evening and adds that the White House pointed it to the president's comments earlier in the week, "when he told reporters that he didn't think he'd bring up the subject during his upcoming meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping". Politico prints both sentences that evening as a White House official's; the Journal prints the second as the White House's statement, and CNN as told to it (its own chip of that day). A White House official tells CNN that the president "maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position". The Spectator recalls that the president disclosed the month before that he had bought and sold Nvidia stock, and that the White House said independent managers had made the trades and there were "no conflicts of interest"; the page gives the reply no day. The Spectator recalls its AI plan of July 2025: the plan declares "the AI race is America's to win" and promised to export America's "full AI technology stack"; by the Spectator's account the White House accepted Nvidia's argument that blocking American chips would send Chinese developers to Huawei. Reuters reports, as Yahoo carries it: "Senior White House officials are discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out in the wake of the spy scandal", "two people familiar with the situation said on Thursday". The White House did not at once answer Reuters's request for comment on his future; an official said of the criticism that the president "maintains complete confidence in the secretary" (the statement on its other chip of that day). CNN reports that there "are now questions brewing inside the White House over why the Commerce Department did not put Megaspeed on" the entity list, "at least while the investigation was ongoing, according to a person familiar". The report names no official and gives the questions no day
Justice Department and the FBI
Benzinga, as Webull carries it on the day of the first report, recalls "the March 2026 DOJ indictment involving Super Micro Computer" and another company: a short seller had cited it in May when it "linked Megaspeed to a suspected server-smuggling network" (the short seller's allegation). Benzinga adds that earlier in October a contractor for Super Micro "pleaded guilty to helping illegally export Nvidia AI chip-powered servers to China as part of an alleged $2.5 billion scheme". The Journal's first report recalls the arrest of March the next day (the Journal's act of Oct 30). The department's own announcement, dated March 19, 2026, is saved: an indictment charging three people with conspiring to divert servers "assembled in the United States and integrating sophisticated U.S. artificial intelligence technology to China"
CBS, as Breitbart relays it: its National Security Division is investigating Megaspeed. A spokeswoman tells the Times the department does not comment on continuing investigations; it declines to comment to NBC, and the FBI declines to comment to AFP and to Semafor on the president's remark that it is looking into the matter
Mother Jones reports that the FBI, "along with the Justice Department's national security division", is investigating Megaspeed over chip shipments to China and "looking into whether China recruited Alice Huang to spy". The FBI declines to comment when the BBC asks, as a Ukrainian outlet relays it; Yahoo Finance also reports an FBI refusal, without saying who asked. CNN reports, as a local station carries it, that the FBI "first raised concerns to lawmakers that Alice Huang might be feeding information to China nearly a year ago", from two people familiar with the matter
Attorney General Blanche tells reporters, of the woman in the reports, that there are "no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me, or by [FBI] Director Patel around who she is or is not"; that she is a spy is "something I have never said and that I don't know to be true"; says "of course" the FBI is investigating the reports. Asked at the same press conference whether he shares concerns that the Commerce Department "was impeding the ability to uncover the smuggling network", he says: "I don't have concerns with the Commerce Department", and "We have a good relationship with the Commerce Department" (RedState that afternoon; the question and the answer in a transcript a commentator posted the next day). CNN, reporting his answer, adds that "The FBI has been investigating Huang's affair for at least a year". Bloomberg, as Quartz relays it: the department "is examining whether entities tied to Alice Huang ... had a hand in attempts to smuggle Super Micro Computer's products into China"; the U.S. attorney's office in Manhattan leads; the department and that office had no comment. Quartz adds that Jensen Huang "is not a target of U.S. law enforcement probes", and that it "remains uncertain" whether the inquiry connects to any smuggling prosecution and what part Alice Huang or her entities had; "Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing", it adds. Reuters, as the Star-Advertiser carries it: a spokesperson for that office "declined to comment on the Bloomberg report". The Seoul Economic Daily, in an article it marks as translated by machine, recalls the department's announcement of March 19 that a Super Micro executive "had been arrested and indicted on charges of smuggling Nvidia semiconductors into China", and says the department suspects Megaspeed was involved in that case; "Super Micro denies the allegations", it adds. The indictment is recalled in these days from Oct 29 (Benzinga: the department's chip of that day) and Oct 30 (the Journal's first report). Semafor reports, from two administration officials, that "Multiple US Justice Department probes threaten to sweep up Nvidia": "One of those probes, on antitrust grounds, is focused specifically on the chipmaker", while "two other inquiries focus on tech companies Megaspeed and Supermicro" and "have focused on the involvement of Alice Huang". It adds: "There's no indication that the DOJ would seek to charge Nvidia, or Huang, criminally at this time". Spokespeople for the department and for Nvidia "didn't provide a comment to Semafor"; a Supermicro spokesperson tells it that "Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer". CBS News reports that it "would not comment about the investigation" of Nvidia's chip sales to Megaspeed, which the Commerce bureau opened in 2024 and which, "according to The New York Times", "was abruptly transferred to the Department of Justice". CBS first published the page on the evening of Nov 12 and updated it the next morning; ANI, crediting CBS, relays the refusal in a page stamped 8:53 a.m. on Nov 13 in India, which is 10:23 p.m. Eastern on Nov 12 ("The DOJ has declined to comment on the matter"), so it stood in the report on its first day
Nvidia company statements
CNBC, Nov 9: Nvidia is "an investor in the Claude creator and counts the AI lab as a significant customer"; Anthropic announced the investment on Nov 18, 2025: "NVIDIA and Microsoft are committing to invest up to $10 billion and up to $5 billion respectively in Anthropic", and "Anthropic's compute commitment will initially be up to one gigawatt of compute capacity with NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems" (five days after the report that it backed a bill to curb Nvidia's exports: the two companies' other line); one of seven companies that agreed to buy $26B of Anthropic stock, Nov 10; CNBC's live page (Nov 12): "the chipmaker has agreed to purchase another $10 billion worth of its Class N common stock immediately following the offering, Anthropic said in an amended prospectus on Tuesday", in "a private placement that will not be registered in the offering" (the page does not say how that sum stands to the $26B); WTOP, Nov 12: as finance chief, Nvidia's interim chief "was a key architect in financing deals with many of Nvidia's biggest customers that include AI titans from Anthropic to CoreWeave". Hunterbrook (dated Nov 10 here and on the other lines that cite it, by the day of first publication in its page data, which the table of pages follows; the page itself prints "November 6, 2026 9:15 AM EST", and which stamp is right is not settled), on the financing Nvidia gives its customers: "the Wall Street Journal reported that Lambda, a privately held cloud computing company backed by Nvidia, has a $35 billion deal to provide computing to Anthropic at the facility" in Texas of which "The Financial Times identified Nvidia as the tenant"; "Nvidia will provide the chips", and "The terms under which Nvidia would share any of Lambda's revenues aren't disclosed". The same article: "The Information recently reported that Nvidia is in talks to potentially provide more than $5 billion in guarantees for another data center Nscale is building", "even though Anthropic has a $45 billion contract with Nscale for this facility" (talks, not a guarantee given)
An earlier public clash over chip-export controls, as CNBC reported it on May 1, 2025. Anthropic had argued in a post of the day before for tighter controls and enforcement ("Maintaining America's compute advantage through export controls is essential for national security and economic prosperity"), saying smugglers had hidden chips in "prosthetic baby bumps" and "packed alongside live lobsters". A Nvidia spokesperson answered: "American firms should focus on innovation and rise to the challenge, rather than tell tall tales that large, heavy, and sensitive electronics are somehow smuggled in" such ways, and: "America cannot manipulate regulators to capture victory in AI"; The Register's update of May 1 gives the first sentence of that reply, which it says Nvidia sent in response to Anthropic's note: "China, with half of the world's AI researchers, has highly capable AI experts at every layer of the AI stack". An Anthropic spokesperson told Fortune: "National security is bigger than the interest of any single company", and that it "stands by its recently filed public submission in support of strong and balanced export controls". That submission, of Apr 29, 2025, says "Anthropic strongly supports" the rule and recommends "export restrictions on certain model weights"; its own words are "packing GPUs alongside live lobsters", and its footnote for the baby bumps cites a press report of 2022 about "over 200 Intel Alder Lake CPUs". Anthropic's own pages give its positions through that year: on Mar 6 it advocated "tightening semiconductor export restrictions", "controlling H20 chips" among them; on Jul 23 it wrote that "we are concerned with the Administration's recent reversal on export of the Nvidia H20 chips to China" and urged the administration "to maintain controls on the H20 chip"; on Oct 21 its chief executive wrote that the real risk is "filling the PRC's data centers with US chips they can't make themselves". On Nov 13, 2025 Reuters, relaying the Wall Street Journal, reported that the GAIN AI Act, legislation "to further curb chipmaker Nvidia's ability to export chips to China", "is also backed by AI startup Anthropic"; Reuters "could not immediately verify the report", Anthropic did not immediately respond to it, and Nvidia had said the bill "stands to restrict global competition for advanced chips". Five days later Anthropic announced Nvidia's investment in it (the two companies' money line)
Its spokesman tells the Times, for the first report: "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year". The Times adds that the company "has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China", and that the spokesman said China's government has "blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry". CNBC, that day: it says Huang's interactions with Megaspeed's officials are not unusual and that the chip-diversion allegations about it were "debunked last year". In its statement to several outlets that day: "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know"; "We often receive updates from the U.S. government regarding parties and entities of concern and always act accordingly" (Tom's Hardware); the spokesperson adds, in CNBC's account, that customers do not get access to its trade secrets or to relevant national security information. A spokesperson tells Tom's Guide: "Building American AI infrastructure worldwide has been a core U.S. policy goal of every Administration. Attacking American industry for honoring longstanding U.S. law and policy undercuts national security"; "The PRC government is not seeking NVIDIA products from regional clouds. Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history"; its regional cloud customers receive "ordinary business information" and "zero information relevant to national security". The Times, in its first report: "The company continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner". Bloomberg, on Nov 9: "Today, Megaspeed remains an official Nvidia Cloud Partner", a designation "that Nvidia generally takes away from companies when they no longer do business with those firms"; Reuters, on Nov 10: it "lists Megaspeed as an official cloud partner on its directory". Sen. Bennet, in a letter released on Nov 11: "As of October 29, 2026, Nvidia continued to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner"
A spokesman tells the Journal that the photographs of Huang with Alice Huang were taken at meetings that included other Nvidia cloud partners in Asia (the sentence is not in an earlier version of the article, timed Oct 30 in a licensed copy; it is in the version the Journal's page dates Oct 31)
The Financial Times reports that in recent months it "has told cloud computing clients that they must now sell at least 51 per cent of their services to non-Chinese companies", on the word of five people; that the instructions "have been communicated verbally", apply to its clients worldwide and to future contracts only; and, from two people, that it "implemented the new requirement over the summer in a pre-emptive effort to reduce the kind of criticism it routinely receives from US lawmakers and other critics of its approach to China". Its reply in the report: "Data centres and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide. Longstanding US policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can. America's longstanding policy has always supported the build-out of American infrastructure worldwide, bringing prosperity, influence and jobs home". The next day a spokesperson, in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation, "did not confirm or deny the verbal requirement", and Invezz relays a follow-up by The Information: the instructions "were intended to encourage a broader customer mix and were not being enforced as a mandatory restriction". Bloomberg, on Nov 6, has it "telling buyers not to rent more than half of their Nvidia computing power to Chinese companies", and writes that the spokesperson "didn't explain the reasoning behind the new Nvidia measure"
The Information reports, as the Daily Caller relays it, that the company "used its influence within the Trump administration to lobby conservative think tanks in Washington", and that one think tank was told its donation was a "tough sell internally" after "a fellow criticized the tech company's relationship with China". The relay names no think tank and gives the lobbying no day. A spokesperson, in a statement to the Daily Caller News Foundation for its report on OpenAI's silence about chip sales to China: "NVIDIA is the vanguard of America's effort to win the AI race and proud to honor longstanding U.S. policy"; "America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide"
Says customer meetings are "part of a CEO's job" and that customers get "zero information relevant to national security"; a spokesman tells the Times Huang "has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed"; the spokesman declines to comment on whether Huang will appear before the committees. In the same statement, to CNBC: "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know". PrimeXBT, on Nov 11, gives as from "a statement reported by CNBC on Nov. 5": "America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide"; the saved CNBC page of that day does not hold the sentence, which the company gave the Daily Caller News Foundation the day before (its chip of Nov 4)
A spokesman tells the Times the company does not share classified information with its customers, and that customers do not ask it to press the government to change its policies on chip sales to China; China has "consistently promoted its own domestic alternatives in China, including Huawei, and strictly limited imports of our data center products". The Times adds that he "has maintained" that Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were not unusual "and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia's many customers". To the FT, for its report of that day, the company "declined to comment on the government memo and the assertions that its chief executive had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang". The FT adds that the company "has previously said" he meets "thousands of customer executives every year"; NBC's account of Nov 8 gives those words as part of its response to the FT. Bloomberg, in an account of Nov 9 that Business Standard carries, says the company "said in a statement after the Nov. 6 New York Times article" that its cloud partners "do not ask us to seek changes in US law or advocate for sales to China", and added: "we trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us" (CBS has that sentence from the company on Nov 8: its chip of that day). By the same account, "In response to the Financial Times report about a possible romantic relationship, Nvidia referred to previous comments by Jensen Huang about having a typical business relationship with Alice Huang". Bloomberg gives neither response a day. Bloomberg reports, as The Edge carries it, that in Southeast Asia it "now requires customers in the region to enrol in its so-called fleet intelligence system", which tracks where participating companies' AI accelerators are, "in order to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners", according to people familiar with the matter; its idea, they say, is "to encourage broader uptake of what remains a voluntary chip tracking programme". The report adds that the system "does not by default require participants to share location data with Nvidia or the US government". Tom's Hardware, relaying the report that day, writes that Nvidia "was not immediately available for comment"; its reply to Bloomberg's questions is on its other chip of that day.
