A representative tells The National, for its report of that day on the committees' letter, that the company has a robust security team that travels with its chief executive "when needed" and always acts accordingly when the government tells it of entities of concern; the paper says the representative "did not say whether Mr Huang would agree to attend". It prints beside this two sentences of the company's statement of the day before; whether its answers to the paper were a separate exchange the page does not say. Bloomberg reports, as The Edge carries it, that since it "pledged in December 2025 to visit Megaspeed's data centres again in the near future" it "has repeatedly declined to say whether such checks have occurred"; asked "again this week whether Nvidia had conducted any additional checks that would support its CEO's assertions" about counting every processor, "a spokesperson declined to comment"; and it "declined to comment on this question or answer others for this story", the question being whether partners that already hold its cloud-partner label, Megaspeed among them, must enrol in its tracking system; among the others, Bloomberg writes, is "whether the new NCP requirement would be applied in regions beyond Southeast Asia" (the new requirement is on its other chip of that day)
A spokesman tells the Times, for its report on licences for chip sales to Chinese firms: "it makes no sense for the Chinese military to depend on American technology"; Nvidia sells "the first, best and most of our technology in America"; and China has strictly limited imports of the chip
Tells CNBC: "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption" (Business Insider, in a profile stamped early on Nov 9, gives the same two sentences as what "a company spokesperson told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday"; its Polish edition repeats them on Nov 10). Tells CBS: "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us". A spokesman tells the Times that Huang will not take part in choosing the outside counsel
Bloomberg reports, about an act of 2025: Nvidia's general counsel "intervened in a US government probe" of Megaspeed, calling a Commerce under secretary in late summer 2025 to ask about it. In Bloomberg's report, as the Business Times of Singapore carries it, a company spokesperson says the general counsel was unaware of the affair when he made the call. Asked by Bloomberg about the company's intervention in the bureau's probe, the spokesperson says that it consults with government officials "to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions and ask whether they have any follow-ups" (words its spokesman also gives the Times that day: its other chip), and: "Unresolved questions about lawful business undercut longstanding US policy and hurt American economic and national security". A spokesman tells the Times the company consults with officials "to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions", and works "to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers". At its event in Seoul that day, asked about the investigation and Korea's chip purchases, declines to comment: "Those questions don't seem to be related to today's event"; asked again whether a senior director of the company, whose visit to Korea had been cancelled, had been due to attend, it says "It is difficult for us to comment because" she "was unable to attend" (Asia Economy). A spokesman declines to comment to the Times, which asked on Monday for its report on succession and the board. To the FT it declines to comment on remarks the paper attributes to its general counsel. To Bloomberg Law, for its report of that day on the company's lobbying team, it "declined to comment about its influence team". Reuters's report of that day on the chip bills, in the copy saved, its automated French translation, calls it the main opponent of two of the bills on the word of a former congressional staffer, and says: "Nvidia n'a pas souhaité faire de commentaire" (it did not wish to comment). By the same report an industry council that "compte notamment Nvidia parmi ses membres" (counts Nvidia among its members) "s'est opposé à ces mesures" (opposed the measures), and its spokeswoman "a refusé de commenter la situation actuelle de Nvidia" (refused to comment on Nvidia's present situation). Beside it the report quotes the spokesman of Americans for Responsible Innovation, which it calls a Washington nonprofit "favorable à ces mesures" (in favour of the measures), and to which Open Philanthropy has made awards (the tie lines give them): "L'obstacle que ces projets de loi doivent surmonter est d'obtenir le soutien de la Maison Blanche" (the obstacle these bills must overcome is winning the White House's support), and it would be "coûteux pour la Maison Blanche de soutenir Nvidia dans un bras de fer avec le Congrès" (costly for the White House to back Nvidia in a standoff with Congress). The FT reports, from people familiar with the situation, that its general counsel insisted inside the company the week before that claims of an affair were inaccurate, saying the sources had "an axe to grind with Jensen" and "They are laundering salacious gossip"; what the company told the FT about them is on its other act of that day. In a statement to The National, for its report of that day: "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead", and his tenure would continue "without interruption" (the words of its statement to CNBC the day before). Bloomberg reports, as the Business Times of Singapore carries it, an earlier call: about three months before, its general counsel told a White House official, according to a person familiar with the call, that Alice Huang "is not as important in Megaspeed as she makes herself out to be", and that Nvidia had stopped doing business with Megaspeed because of the bad publicity around her. Daring Fireball quotes a Bloomberg report of Dec 22, 2025: Nvidia "told Bloomberg that it went to Megaspeed's facilities multiple times to verify that there's nothing untoward", and a spokesperson said in mid-November 2025: "Our visits confirmed that the GPUs shipped to Megaspeed by our partners are where they are supposed to be". Fortune, listing what it calls "the multiple questionable statements made by Jensen Huang and his company since 2025", recalls two of the company's. In October 2025, when the Times reported that Huang and Alice Huang had been seen drinking together at an industry event, a spokesman said, as the Times printed it then: "Our field operations teams often host groups of customers and partners at conferences, and when Jensen is available, may ask him to visit to provide updates on the market" (Fortune shortens this to "When Jensen is available, [customers] may ask him to visit to provide updates on the market", which makes customers the ones who ask). In December 2025, when Bloomberg reported the investigation of Megaspeed, the company said Megaspeed was "a cloud service permitted under the export control rules"; Bloomberg, recalling that statement on Nov 9, says a spokesperson also said then that the company's own review "had found no evidence of diversion" on Megaspeed's part and showed the firm was "fully owned and operated outside of China, with no China shareholders", and quotes: "When the law is clear, American companies honor US laws as they are, not as America's critics wish they were". CNBC reports, from the company's disclosures, that it spent "a record $2.15 million on federal lobbying in the third quarter", and that its "$4.69 million in 2026 lobbying expenses through September nearly matches the $4.97 million it spent in all of 2025". The totals are for all its federal lobbying; the report ties no sum to a decision. Bloomberg Law, that day, from the same disclosures: the company said it lobbied on issues "related to semiconductor trade policy and artificial intelligence" and on export controls, that it "also disclosed lobbying on quantum computing and energy matters in the third quarter", and that it "lobbied the US Senate and House and executive branch agencies, including the Pentagon, Commerce and Treasury departments, the National Security Council, and others"; beside its in-house lobbyists it retained three outside firms in the third quarter, and a firm it had retained before "filed a termination report effective July 31". ZeroHedge, after listing smuggling charges and reports since and Megaspeed's renting of data-centre capacity to Alibaba, writes that these make "Nvidia's response from last December age like milk", and reprints its own post of Dec 10, 2025 with that response in headline form: "HAVEN'T RECEIVED TIPS OF 'PHANTOM DATACENTERS'", "SMUGGLING SEEMS FARFETCHED", "NVIDIA SAYS IT PURSUES ANY TIPS IT RECEIVES". PC Gamer, on Nov 12, gives the words as the company's answer at the time to the claim that a Chinese model was trained on its Blackwell chips: "While such smuggling seems far-fetched, we pursue any tip we receive"
Declines to comment to the Times for its profile of Alice Huang. A spokesperson tells the FT, for its report on the delayed listing of Megaspeed: "we placed Megaspeed on our block list in June 2025, prohibiting any further sales or shipments"; "That voluntary block remains in place". A spokesman tells the Journal, of its general counsel's call to the export bureau: "we have an obligation to resolve any potential 'red flags' before proceeding"; that the ban on sales to Megaspeed is still in place, that Commerce has not blacklisted the company, and that Nvidia got the bureau's permission for parts and replacement components sent since; and that U.S. intelligence officials never gave Huang a warning that he might be a target. Al Jazeera recalls that it welcomed the president's approval, in December 2025, of sales of its H200 chip to China, saying the decision would "support high-paying jobs and manufacturing in America". 24/7 Wall St., as Yahoo Finance carries it, sets beside a short seller's allegation of May, that Chinese demand still drove over 20% of its compute revenue "through illegal diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries", the company's earlier statement: "NVIDIA had said its China compute business went to zero after the April 2025 export restrictions". Axios reports, as Raw Story relays it that day, that some export approvals came before the warning its report describes: "Nvidia disclosed an H200 export license in February". Legal Insurrection quotes Axios's sentence the next day. CNBC recalls that in 2025 it "changed the way it reported regional sales to categorize by customer headquarters, instead of by where the products were billed", and "also stopped reporting Singapore sales during the same period". The Journal's column of the next evening quotes the filings (the Journal's act of Nov 11). The Information reports on Tuesday, Nov 10, as Gizmodo relays it that day, that Alice Huang's relationship with Huang and the company "helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies since 2023" (the report cites people familiar with the matter). In a statement to The Information, in Gizmodo's words, a spokesperson says the company "primarily sells its data center GPUs through established partners and works with them to ensure compliance with U.S. export controls", "applies the same standards to all transactions", and that "its due diligence and cooperation with law enforcement have helped uncover suspected efforts to evade export restrictions, resulting in federal prosecutions". The Daily Caller News Foundation has the statement in the company's own words the next day (its chip of Nov 11)
Declines to give the Times a statement for its report of a second relationship; declines to comment for another Times article and for an FT report of that day; declines to answer the Journal's questions, for its column of that evening, on where its sales to Megaspeed were classified under its old and new ways of reporting revenue by country, and on whether the end of its separate line for Singapore was related to its block of Megaspeed. For the Daily Caller News Foundation's account of The Information's report of the day before, that Alice Huang "used her ties to the Nvidia CEO and the company's distributors to help move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to Chinese tech firms since 2023", a spokesperson tells it: "We sell our data-center GPUs primarily to well-known partners", "who work with us to ensure that all sales comply with U.S. export control rules"; "Our due diligence has helped identify suspected attempts to circumvent U.S. export controls, leading to federal prosecutions" (Gizmodo has the statement as given to The Information: its chip of Nov 10). The Wire China, in a profile of Alice Huang published that day: "Jensen Huang is committed to staying on as Nvidia's chief executive, according to a company spokesperson", who added: "America's longstanding policy has always supported the buildout of American infrastructure worldwide, bringing prosperity, influence, and jobs home". The profile gives the statement no day and names no one it was made to; the saved copy was modified on Nov 13. The second sentence stands, spelt "build-out", in the company's reply to the FT of Nov 2 (its chip of that day), and the first matches its statement of Nov 8 that he "is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption"; whether the profile repeats those statements or reports a new one, the page does not say
A spokesperson clarifies, in NBC's report of the resignation, that Huang will not be working with Nvidia in any capacity going forward. The Journal, in another piece of that day, repeats that it "has declined to say how Megaspeed's sales were classified" after it changed how it reports revenue by country (the refusal, to the Journal's column of the evening before, is on its act of Nov 11); Implicator adds that the filings "do not establish a connection between the reporting change and the block". Declines to comment to the FT and the Journal for other reports of that day, and to Reuters for its report that afternoon that Huang "had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter"; Reuters does not name the employee. Tells a nonprofit that found accounts on X defending Huang in what the Washington Post calls an apparent effort that it was aware of the accounts and was trying to identify the source; it did not respond to the Post. TechCrunch's timeline of that day recounts its statements of October 2025, when the investigations of Megaspeed were confirmed: it did not have "any reason to believe products had been diverted", and "NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed - Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules". VentureBeat recalls, in an article on what the resignation means for the financing of AI data centres, its answer to a Reuters investigation of Oct 1 that found lenders wanting stronger guarantees for deals it backs: it "defended its approach, saying outside financing partners independently evaluate customer commitments, anticipated cash flows and equipment resale values". The New York Post, in its report of that day on the Commerce Department, as AOL carries it: it "has been applying immense pressure on Commerce not to impose stricter limits", "putting agency leaders in a bind as they also try to appease China hawks within the administration", according to the chief executive of a research firm, whom the paper names; he gives no occasion. In the same report its spokesperson says that it regularly consults with "BIS, [the Office of Export Enforcement], and other officials to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions, and ask whether they have any follow-ups" (the words it gave the Times and Bloomberg on Nov 9)
Jensen Huang founder and chief executive
Trump gave him the National Medal of Science, Oct 2026; he flew to China on Air Force One, May 2026
Tells Bloomberg, as Taiwan News relays the interview (Bloomberg's saved page shows its opening only): "Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual"; as Data Center Knowledge relays it, "We've studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one". Data Center Dynamics has him calling the story "groundless speculation". Quartz relays more of it: "And I think the U.S. government also has as well"; and he said the U.S. government had not told him of its suspicions about her. Yahoo Finance, which carries the Bloomberg report under its reporters' names, has him speak "in an interview Thursday" and say one thing more of her: "She's no longer with Megaspeed, he said". Political.org recalls, in its background to the first report: "in May 2025 Jensen Huang said there was no evidence of any AI chip diversion". SemiAnalysis, on Nov 12, quotes him "at Computex in May 2025": "There's no evidence of any AI chip diversion", and "The important thing is that the countries and the companies that we sell to recognize that diversion is not allowed and everybody would like to continue to buy Nvidia technology"; it sets after the quotation "at least two high profile counter examples". The quotation as it prints it opens with a sentence about counting deployments that Data Center Knowledge gives as from his Bloomberg interview of Oct 29 (his other chip of that day)
Memo to staff: "I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife"; "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry"; to his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders: "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility"; on the board's inquiry: "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully"; "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence". In the same memo: "I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security"; and, as the Times quotes its end: "My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do". Al Jazeera recalls that in August 2025 "the Trump administration announced it would take a 15 percent cut of certain Nvidia chip sales to China"; PC Gamer, the next day: the president "said he'd do it in return for 15% of their China revenue". The Spectator, on Nov 12, recounts the bargain: when the president wanted 20 percent of the revenue from sales of the H20 chip to China, "Huang talked him down to 15"; it quotes the president: "So we negotiated a little deal"
Pulls out of speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum, in TechCrunch's timeline; Business Insider, as The Coin Republic relays it, dates the withdrawal to Nov 9. Wired reports, as TechCrunch and SiliconANGLE relay it that day, that he hired a crisis-communications firm "at least a year before he publicly acknowledged" the relationship; CNBC, Nov 11: the firm he "reportedly hired as early as last year". By the president's account that Monday, tells him by phone that he "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy". Apologises to his staff at headquarters that Monday and then runs his meetings "as if it were business as usual", in Fortune's account, which cites CNBC. CNBC, saying the reports "prompted renewed scrutiny" of his past comments on the Chinese market, recalls what he told it on Oct. 22: "No market is closed forever, and China wants foreign companies to invest in China, just as Germany wants foreign companies and countries to invest in Germany"; "There's no reason to believe that market is going to be closed to the best competitors in the world". TechCrunch recalls that he "has publicly lamented export controls", calling them a "failure" at a conference in 2025 and saying in May that it was "not wise" for the U.S. and China to create two distinct AI ecosystems; and that he has warned that shutting Nvidia out of China's market would let the country develop chips to challenge it. Slate, the same day, has him calling the previous administration's policies a failure "that had cost Nvidia and other U.S. companies billions". Emptywheel quotes a news account of the company's gift to the White House ballroom in October 2025: he told reporters at the time that the company was contributing "in a small way" and gave no amount; "Documents show Nvidia requested that its $25 million donation be kept anonymous". CNN recalls, in an article on whether Nvidia can do without him, that Huang "has said he never believed in succession planning", telling a podcaster earlier in the year "that he hoped to die at his desk". Its live page of Nov 11 gives the remark as a hope to die "on the job", with the reason he gave: the best way, in his view, is "to prepare everyone at the company", passing on "knowledge, information, insight, skills, experience as often and continuously as you can, which is why I continuously reason about everything in front of my team"
Axios reports, as Raw Story relays it that day, among approvals that came before the warning its report describes: he "told Axios in March that the company held licenses covering Chinese customers". Legal Insurrection quotes Axios's sentence the next day
Reached by phone by the Times and asked about a second relationship: "I don't think you should be talking to me directly"; "He then hung up", the Times writes. By Rep. Mast's account to reporters, tentatively agrees that Wednesday night to testify before Congress (CNN). ANI reports, giving no day, that he "addressed the matter during a closed-door staff meeting, expressed regret and did not take questions before moving on to regular business discussions"; Fortune describes an apology to his staff on Monday, Nov 9 (his chip of that day), and the pages do not say whether this is that meeting. Semafor, in a review of 42 of his podcast interviews since 2022 for which it "used a pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI to score each" exchange on his stance, finds that before the limits of early 2025 he "spoke on podcasts about export restrictions in a largely neutral tenor, framing them as a matter of compliance", and that afterwards he argued "that the restrictions hurt the US more than China"; it quotes what he told one host in May 2025: "If we leave a market altogether, there's no question somebody else would step in". CNN's live page recalls that evening an interview with Bloomberg filmed a few weeks before the reports: his hope that the "next leader of the company is already at the company", and: "Just as I can be fired the next CEO has to be hired", "I like that we can't be overly complacent about our position inside the company". NPR, the FT and Business Today quote the same interview the next day; NPR calls him "vague about succession plans" and quotes him: "I'm really hoping that the next CEO of the company is already at the company, but 20 years from now, I hope I stay healthy and I hope I continue to earn my keep". What he had told a podcaster earlier in the year is on his chip of Nov 9. By the president's account in an interview the next day, calls him that Wednesday: "I spoke to him yesterday. He's going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That's what he told me", and "he called me as the president" (a transcript of the interview). The FT: "The president said he spoke to Huang on Wednesday as his position at Nvidia was unravelling"
Resigns after 33 years as chief executive, and with it as president and as a member of the board (announced Nov 12; the company's filing says that on Nov 11 the board "accepted the resignation" of Huang "as NVIDIA's President, Chief Executive Officer and member of the Board, effective immediately"). CNBC confirms a Times report that he has hired the law firm Paul Weiss: "It's not immediately clear what he will use its services for". CBC recalls his case for looser controls and quotes what he told the Associated Press in June: "We have to, No. 1, make sure that we have national security and that we protect our nation, but we also simultaneously should go and compete, and grow our technology industry and maximize our exports"
Nvidia board of directors
Opens an independent investigation; says it "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised" and "has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team"; its inquiry "will examine all available information", and it "will provide further updates as appropriate". In the same statement: "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders"
Hires outside counsel: its independent members say in a statement of that day that they "have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York", whom the statement names, "and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation as was announced on Sunday"
Meets to discuss removing Huang. CNBC, from a person familiar with the matter: it decided that night to oust him and made the decision official the next morning. Bloomberg reports, as Semafor and Daring Fireball relay it, that Nvidia has hired an outside search firm to find its next chief and that the board is weighing a temporary one. Semafor adds, from people familiar with the matter and an administration official: some directors favour naming Kress interim chief if Huang is removed, it briefed the White House on its planned meeting, and Apple's hardware chief is among those being considered
Names Kress interim chief, Jones chair; begins a search for a permanent chief, for which it "will consider internal and external candidates" (announced Nov 12; the company's filing dates Jones's appointment to Nov 11 and gives no day for Kress's). The release says Kress keeps her duties as chief financial officer and that results will be reported on Nov 17 "as previously scheduled". Quartz reports, crediting the company, that Jones "will direct the search for a permanent CEO". In the release on the resignation: "Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound"; "The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry". Electronics Weekly, a British trade paper, reports that Thursday that the board "is meeting today to decide if CEO Jensen Huang should be replaced and, if so, by who"; the page does not say whether that is the session of Wednesday night, U.S. time. Semafor's report of the night before, in a version changed that morning, adds that the board "has debated whether, as part of its potential replacement of Huang, to introduce a chief operating officer to serve alongside the interim chief executive"
Colette Kress chief financial officer; interim chief, announced Nov 12
Statement: "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created"; "We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI"; "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders". In an email to staff: "this has been an extraordinarily difficult period". CNBC, from a person familiar with the matter: she "will gather the company's executive team today" at headquarters to "discuss leadership and continuity plans". In the same email to staff: "I believe deeply in this company and in its future"; "we will host a company meeting on November 18"
Harvey Jones director; board chair, appointed Nov 11 and announced Nov 12
Statement: "Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position"; "She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA's strategy and advancing its technology roadmap" (his sentence on the board's confidence is on his other chip of that day). In a note to employees: "The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company"; "I am confident that under Colette's leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business". In the release on the appointment: "The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption"
Shareholders suing Nvidia a class action
Complaint filed in federal court, a proposed class action for those who bought the company's securities "between October 9, 2025 and November 8, 2026, both dates inclusive": it says that statements of a company spokesman about Megaspeed and about Huang's dealings with its executive, and Huang's own words in a Bloomberg article of Oct 30, were each "materially false and misleading" when made, because of the affair; the complaint "seeks to recover compensable damages" for shareholders (Kotaku). It demands a trial by jury. These are the plaintiff's allegations
A second complaint is filed in federal court that day, a shareholder derivative suit on the company's behalf "against CEO Jensen Huang and certain current and former directors and executives": it "alleges breaches of fiduciary duty, violations of Section 14(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and unjust enrichment" (a law firm's summary), and that some defendants were "engaging in lucrative insider trading while the Company's stock price was artificially inflated", "netting combined total proceeds of approximately $2,000,000,000" (the complaint's allegation). A litigation tracker notes the next day that the complaint "also alleges that some defendants engaged in insider trading (a claim not alleged in the 1st lawsuit)". The complaint demands a trial by jury
Nvidia shares
Falls more than 4%
Falls 5.47%
Slides about 10% in early trading, in Al Jazeera's account; 13% at the open, in the FT's
AMD and Broadcom shares of two rival chip makers
Both among the seven that agreed to buy Anthropic stock, Nov 10. Hunterbrook (Nov 10) likens Nvidia's customer financing to "Broadcom's financing arrangement with Anthropic, which uses Alphabet's TPUs, in that both aim to help customers access computing capacity while encouraging reliance on a particular chip supplier"; it gives the arrangement no amount and no date. In Fortune (Nov 11) the chief AI officer of a consulting firm writes that "Anthropic recently demonstrated that it could move its inference workloads from Nvidia's CUDA software stack to AMD in just three days, suggesting that Nvidia's software moat may no longer be as strong as it once was"; that is his account, in a note on what the resignation means for the market. CNBC's live page (Nov 12) names Anthropic first among five companies at which "AMD's Helios is now deployed", OpenAI among them; it gives the deployment no day
AMD up 13%, Broadcom up 10%
Anthropic the company at far left
At Davos in January its chief executive likened selling advanced chips to China to "selling nuclear weapons to North Korea", TechCrunch recalls (an essay of his that its page dates January 2026 has it in writing, of selling chips to China's ruling party: "this is like selling nuclear weapons to North Korea and then bragging that the missile casings are made by Boeing"); the Times, on Nov 10, adds that Huang "pushed back on the analogy": "Lunacy", on a podcast this year. In June 2025, by Fortune, Huang had said of him at a press briefing in Paris: "he believes that AI is so scary that only they should do it", and "Don't do it in a dark room and tell me it's safe"; an Anthropic spokesperson answered that he "has never claimed that" only Anthropic "can build safe and powerful AI"
TechCrunch (Nov 12) recalls that it and OpenAI "have reportedly appealed directly to Washington" over alleged theft of their models by Chinese labs, "urging stronger protections", and calls Huang "the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons". The same article gives the letter behind that: "Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China", and "The impetus for that letter was Washington's debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI"
Decrypt (Nov 12) reports an open-source advocate's allegation of that day that it and OpenAI "have spent millions lobbying the US Congress to ban open weights" and formed a group "to push for strict limits on open models"; Decrypt says the broader claim "needs, of course, much more evidence", that the initiative he points to, Pacing the Frontier, "is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang", and that its chief executive "said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban". Of what the advocate says Huang built in answer, Decrypt reports in its own voice: "In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance", "which works on open AI security tools and standards", and "Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions"; why the alliance was formed it does not say
A letter of Nov 12 from two senators who are not drawn (Lisa Blunt Rochester and John Curtis) urges the Commerce secretary "to take immediate steps to close loopholes in the export regime for advanced AI chips" and cites the company's work for its account of how China uses the technology: "This is well demonstrated by Anthropic's recent report Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026", in which its "Threat Intelligence team details incidents in which China-based entities and Chinese" "government affiliates used artificial intelligence for cyber operations, surveillance, scams and fraud, conventional weapons, and distillation". The letter gives the report's web address in a footnote; it mentions no contact with the company, and the report itself is not saved here
Its dealings, as a commentator's newsletter of Nov 12 gives them in its notes on the offering (the chips on its row give the offering itself): "Anthropic discloses $10 billion in new deals with Microsoft and Google". The newsletter says neither what those deals are nor how the sum is split, and gives them no day
A charge about its motives. Its first saved occasion is of October 2025: by Axios (Oct 16), the White House's AI adviser, answering an essay by Anthropic's policy chief, claimed that "Anthropic is running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy", one "based on fear-mongering" in his words; Axios asked whether he was "being hypocritical" in saying so, "given that" he "and others on the White House AI policy team hail from monied tech interests in Silicon Valley", and whether Anthropic was "being hypocritical when it expresses "appropriate fear" while spending (and raising) billions for the sake of AI advancement". Five days later its chief executive wrote that "there has been a recent uptick in inaccurate claims about Anthropic's policy stances", and that harming start-ups "makes no sense for us". Then, as pages of 2026 give it. Fortune (Aug 18): an investor said on a podcast that he had been told "by multiple people I trust" that its chief executive had said "Anthropic might be the only private company in the world at some point"; a former White House AI adviser repeated his claim of "regulatory capture", in Fortune's gloss "where Anthropic uses fear of AI's risks to persuade the government to enact stringent regulation on the technology that only Anthropic can easily comply with". Anthropic denied that its chief executive had said it ("Complete and utter nonsense", its communications chief wrote); the adviser, Fortune adds, "later pointed out that" the chief executive "himself did not directly address" the claim; and the chief executive wrote that it tries "very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors". Morningstar, in a note of Nov 12 on its prospectus: "some have suggested these comments carry ulterior motives, accusing frontier AI labs like Anthropic of fear-mongering to secure favorable regulations and drown smaller competitors in legal costs"; it names no one
The government and its models in 2026 (the president's order of February is on another line). A law firm's note: "On June 12, 2026, the US Commerce Department, under Secretary Howard Lutnick's signature, issued" a directive requiring a license for any export or transfer of two of its models, which "followed outreach to senior government officials by a US company raising concerns that researchers had identified a method of bypassing safety guardrails". A security trade outlet: "Commerce partially eased the restriction on June 26", and later "withdrew export controls on Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models following weeks of negotiation". Morningstar (Nov 12): it was "labeled a “supply chain risk” by the Pentagon" and saw "the Commerce Department switch off its flagship models for weeks". Another page on the withdrawal names the company: "The concern that triggered the order originated with Amazon", whose researchers "reported that a series of prompts could get Fable 5 to produce information useful in cyberattacks"; talks between Amazon's chief executive "and the White House helped prompt the directive, The Wall Street Journal reported"; Anthropic "disputed the severity, calling the jailbreak "relatively simple" and replicable on other publicly available models"; the Commerce secretary wrote that "the controls in the June 12 letter are withdrawn". The model that builds this figure is of that family
Sets its IPO price range; seven companies agree to buy $26B of its stock. A newsletter of that day lists among its headlines "Anthropic launches roadshow for proposed initial public offering", and a commentator's newsletter of Nov 12 says "The roadshow has begun"; neither gives the launch a day of its own. Reuters reports, as Techmeme lists it on the morning of Nov 10, that it "sent out and then retracted details of its blockbuster IPO filing, according to emails to bankers seen by Reuters late on Monday"; in Techmeme's summary the copy showed "plans to raise up to ~$69B", and it "then followed up saying the pricing details were inaccurate". Only the listing is cited here: the report itself is not saved, and the listing gives the sending no day of its own
ABC Australia reports, in an entry of its live page stamped 11:50 a.m. Thursday in Sydney, which is 7:50 p.m. Eastern on Nov 11, that it "has lodged its Australian prospectus with ASIC": "Retail investors can apply for new Class A shares, with Nasdaq trading expected to begin on 20 November". The entry gives the lodging no day. It prints beside it a portfolio manager's note on the investment: "There are clear risks around Anthropic's competitive moat, particularly its pricing power", and "The circular financing structure is a red flag for the industry and creates governance risks"
Quartz reports that an Anthropic spokesperson "declined to comment", in its report on Huang's exit and Anthropic's share sale; the page does not say who asked. Semafor reports, in its account of Congress's push to pass three chip-export bills after the affair, that it "has publicly supported all three bills"; the page gives that support no day. The same sentence says OpenAI "has been warming up to them as well after initially being reticent to support the proposals"; a Senate Democratic aide tells Semafor the bills were "buoyed unexpectedly by the Nvidia scandal", and the page adds that Nvidia opposes them and that the broader tech industry "has also lobbied against them". Reuters, relaying the Wall Street Journal, had reported on Nov 13, 2025 that it backed the GAIN AI Act, which this page calls "an earlier version of the AI Overwatch Act", one of the three (the line between the two companies gives the report and its cautions)
OpenAI
Open Philanthropy awarded it $30 million in 2017
The Daily Caller, relaying a report that OpenAI kept quiet on chip sales to China so as not to alienate Nvidia (OpenAI's chip of Nov 4), calls Nvidia its "key supplier"; CNBC reports a "backstop deal Nvidia offered OpenAI" in August, to rent a planned data center campus. Nvidia is also an investor: TechCrunch, Nov 9: "Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave, and Nebius"; Hunterbrook, Nov 10, reading the company's filings, writes of "Nvidia's $30 billion investment in OpenAI, which has not been completely funded yet" and of a "preliminary agreement Nvidia just reached to inject $100 billion of equity in 10 installments into OpenAI, each one tied to OpenAI placing orders for Nvidia chips". And in 2016, by Yahoo Finance (Nov 12), "Huang hand-delivered Nvidia's first DGX-1 AI server to OpenAI, the lab Musk co-founded"; CNN (Nov 9) says Nvidia "donated" it. By the FT (Nov 12), from two people, Nvidia's finance chief, now its interim chief, "has challenged Huang on several decisions, including a $250bn deal to support data centre developments for OpenAI", and "Nvidia ultimately agreed to provide a $100bn backstop with an option to provide the remainder over time"; CNBC, that day, relays a report of The Information that she "was against the $105 billion OpenAI deal". The two accounts give different sums and are not shown to be one occasion; neither gives the objection a day. The New Republic (Nov 12) recalls that "In January 2025, Nvidia was announced as one of the “key” technology partners" in the "initiative to jump-start AI-focused data center development, dubbed the Stargate Project"; its page names neither OpenAI nor its partners, and a conference report of 2025 saved for this figure says "OpenAI announced the Stargate Project, a new venture backed by SoftBank, OpenAI, Oracle and MGX"
TechCrunch (Nov 12) recalls that it and Anthropic "have reportedly appealed directly to Washington" over alleged theft of their models by Chinese labs, "urging stronger protections"; by the same article that debate was "The impetus" for an open letter Huang wrote "Earlier this year", "signed by 25 companies", "urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China". Decrypt (Nov 12) reports an open-source advocate's allegation that the two "have spent millions lobbying the US Congress to ban open weights" and formed a group "to push for strict limits on open models", says the broader claim "needs, of course, much more evidence", that the initiative he points to, Pacing the Frontier, "is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang", and adds that OpenAI "subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter". Of what the advocate says Huang built in answer, Decrypt reports in its own voice: "In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance", "which works on open AI security tools and standards"; why the alliance was formed it does not say
TechCrunch (Nov 9), on how the industry guards its secrets, sets beside the affair "The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer", who "was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room": "OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed", and the article adds that "the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close". The page gives OpenAI's statement no day
Its suppliers and its own financing, as pages of these days give them. Hunterbrook (Nov 10), beside Nvidia's investment in the cloud company CoreWeave: "OpenAI, another investee, also buys CoreWeave compute. To close the loop, OpenAI invested directly in CoreWeave"; it gives neither a day nor a sum. CNBC's live page (Nov 12) names it among five companies at which "AMD's Helios is now deployed", and reports that "OpenAI has raised $15 billion in its latest funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation", on the word of sources, after "originally planning to raise up to $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation in the latest funding effort, before pulling back". A commentator's newsletter of Nov 12 gives another sum, "OpenAI raises $11 billion in funding at $1.25 trillion value"; the pages do not show whether the two are one round. TechCrunch (Nov 12): "some of Nvidia's biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips"
The government and its models in 2026, from the page that reports the end of the controls on Anthropic's: "OpenAI delayed the full public launch of its GPT-5.6 model at the government's request, limiting initial access to vetted partners under a voluntary review framework"; its chief executive said that a testing period mandated by the government "is not a bad idea," but that he did not like "the idea of the government picking the customers"; another page on the end of the controls adds that OpenAI "said it had previewed their capabilities for the government ahead of the launch"
The Information reports on Tuesday, Nov 3, as the Daily Caller relays it the next day, that its executives "have strayed away from declaring a definitive public stance" on advanced chip sales to China "due to concerns that it could alienate chipmaker Nvidia"; the relay's headline: "OpenAI Bit Its Tongue On China Chips To Keep Nvidia Happy". In a statement The Information quotes, its chief global affairs officer says that it "continues to support the strengthening of export controls". The sentence is in its policy paper dated November 2026, which gives no day
Its board chairman, who also runs an AI startup, on a show, as Yahoo Finance quotes him on Nov 10 (it says he spoke "on the same show" as a guest it quotes from Monday): "We lead in AI, and that means leading in power. It means leading in compute. It means leading in chips"; "AI is not particularly popular right now in this country"; "So I think this just introduces even more risk"
Semafor reports that it "has been warming up to" the three chip-export bills before Congress "after initially being reticent to support the proposals"; the same sentence says Anthropic "has publicly supported all three bills". The page gives neither a day
Elon Musk chief executive of Tesla
CNBC: "SpaceX is one of Nvidia's largest customers, and Nvidia invested in SpaceX via an equity investment in Musk's xAI"
Axios, as Implicator relays it from unnamed sources: the president called him from the Oval Office before deciding, and he "supported imposing the controls"
Replies "I agree" to Shaun Maguire's post that Huang is "irreplaceable for America's AI leadership"; the FT: he "backed Huang"
Posts that hiring Huang "would be an honor", in reply to a ZeroHedge post: "Elon please hire Jensen". The post is stamped 8:22 PM Eastern
CNBC reports that, before the resignation, he agreed with an investment manager's post that "Nvidia's board should wait for the results of the investigation before ousting Jensen". Replies "True words" to a post that a founder is not simply replaced, in a Journal column of that day
Shaun Maguire partner at Sequoia Capital
Posts that Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad for America", "but my guess is there was no bad intention", and "Two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership"; Elon Musk replies "I agree"
The FT quotes him: "Yes he should have known better"; "But let's also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op". A blog of that day quotes him on such approaches: "you're drunk and make a mistake and then you're owned"
In a post that a Journal column quotes: "This has nothing to do with money. This is about America winning in AI"
Bill Ackman founder of Pershing Square Capital Management
Posts that Huang "is human. And he is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes", and adds in a reply to his own post that day: "I am not suggesting he gets a free pass. If indeed this is more than an affair", it is "a real problem"; "I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security"
Tim Sweeney chief executive of Epic Games
Posts: "A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity". PC Gamer: he has since called the outcome "far too much government heavy handedness" and, in another post, criticised the new interim chief for waiting a week before discussing everything at a company meeting (the article's paraphrase). Before the resignation, in a comment PC Gamer quotes that day: "This would be an Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy from Nvidia's board if they did that, and a grievous harm to the United States of America"
Jim Cramer host of Mad Money on CNBC
On his show: "A Jensen-less Nvidia is an Nvidia many will not want to own"
On CNBC after the announcement: "It had to happen. There's way too much evidence"; of the interim chief: "I think she's going to be terrific in trying to figure out where the pieces are"; he rejects the idea that the company's other employees have no bearing on its future: "I think that's just not true"; CNBC's report adds his investing club's guidance, "We don't want to step in to buy the stock into this scandal-driven sell-off, but we're not giving up on the company either", and that he suggested the company preannounce its results. In a post that PC Gamer quotes: "Jensen we hardly knew yah. Just plain awful...."
Larry Kudlow host of Kudlow on Fox Business
On his show: "Step down, Mr. Huang. Right now"
Clément Delangue chief executive of Hugging Face
Nvidia agreed in 2026 to acquire his company for about $12.9 billion, CNBC reports; the deal has not closed
Posts: "This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened"; calls it "a really sad day" and adds: "we'll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever"
Changpeng Zhao co-founder of Binance
Posts that it is "a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign"
Ron Conway venture capitalist
Posts: "As the swirl continues (which I believe should be taken seriously), let's pause for a moment and remember what Jensen has contributed to our industry ... Now we should be patient and wait for investigations by the board of directors and any government authorities to conclude"
Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs
Denies the Journal's account of Alice Huang: "no such investigations"; its police say the Megaspeed inquiry continues, that they are "unable to comment further at this juncture", and: "While we do not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, we act firmly against companies and individuals who violate our laws and are engaged in fraudulent and dishonest practices"; the reply adds that Singapore "has charged four individuals and four companies in Court between Feb 2025 and Jul 2026 for committing fraud on suppliers of servers", and says Singapore "does not condone businesses deliberately using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate other countries' export controls" and expects companies there "to take into account other countries' regulations, including export controls". The statement is timed Oct 30, 11:13 PM in Singapore; the ministry's newsroom page dates it Oct 31
Its statement: its police and customs began an independent investigation of several companies, Megaspeed among them, in February 2025, "not based on any request from any country or sovereign entity"; a check at Megaspeed by the U.S. export bureau on 24 June 2025, with her present, "was the first time Singapore came to know about the US's interest in Megaspeed and Huang", and the police interviewed her that day and held her passport; the servers in question "had been purchased by companies (which were under investigation) and exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the Singapore market", and the police force "was investigating whether the servers had subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore"; in Feb 2026 found "insufficient evidence" of offences over the declarations under investigation; its police "assessed that Huang had provided information which she knew to be inaccurate" to them "in the course of investigations, to downplay her role in Megaspeed", and she "was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country" ("Other cases in the past have been dealt with in a similar way"); her passport was returned on 26 February 2026 "and she departed Singapore on the same day"; no espionage investigation. Requests to U.S. authorities for help in getting Supermicro's cooperation, made at "a meeting on 7 July 2025" and repeated "on several occasions" since September 2025 to the Justice Department and the FBI, brought "limited information or assistance"; its investigation of the company and six other individuals continues (its statement and the Journal's live report). The statement opens: Singapore "does not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries", expects companies there "to take into account such regulations", and "does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate other countries' export controls through fraud or dishonest practices". It closes: "We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it"
China's Foreign Ministry
Its spokesman on the Times report: "unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China"
Its spokesman, that Monday, in NBC's account: "the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China". The ministry's transcript of that day's press conference has him asked, by AFP and NBC, to comment on the board's inquiry and Huang's acknowledgment of an affair, and answer: "We responded to that last week", and the allegation "is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China" (The National quotes an official of the ministry in "a video address on Monday": "It is nothing but smears against China"); asked that day how China would respond to tighter curbs on chips: "China's position on the U.S. export of chips to China is consistent. For anything specific, I'd refer you to competent authorities"
At the ministry's press conference, asked whether the two presidents will discuss the allegations: "the two sides are in communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state within the year", and "we've stated China's position on multiple occasions"; asked about Alice Huang's citizenship and whereabouts: "We responded to that yesterday", and the allegation "is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China"
Asked about calls for tighter chip limits: "Our position on U.S. chip exports to China is consistent"
Its spokeswoman: the U.S. should "stop fabricating" spy "narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions"; asked that Thursday about a report that she had returned to China: "I do not have information on what you mentioned" (CBS). Asked at that briefing whether the scandal will affect relations before the two presidents' likely summit, she says the two countries "maintain close communication on heads-of-state interactions". Asked there by AFP about procurement notices showing that a university in Xi'an "bought several NVIDIA H200 chips, despite them being restricted on the U.S. export controls", she says: "I'm not familiar with the specifics you mentioned", and: "China firmly opposes the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security and formulating various types of discriminatory lists to go after Chinese institutions"
Chinese Embassy in Washington
Its spokesman, in the Times: a campaign of "groundless smears and slanders"
In the Journal's report, as a licensed copy timed that day carries it: rejects the allegations, saying China opposes the peddling of a "Chinese spy narrative" and that its technological development is grounded in "independent innovation"
Its spokesman tells the Times its reporting is "unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China"
Megaspeed the Singapore firm in the reports
In a statement to the Times, in its first report: "outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the U.S. government that we are fully committed to cooperating". Later adds, in a further statement the Times prints, that it "cannot respond to a media trial and welcomes formal, evidence-based investigation"
Posts a statement on LinkedIn, in a Dow Jones report of that day: investigations by U.S. authorities and others found "no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities"; it maintains "the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct". The words are those of its statement dated Dec 23, 2025, which another page of that day says it is standing by. The statement also says: "we do not rule out pursuing legal action to protect our reputation and to hold Bloomberg accountable for the misleading nature of the article"; and that "over the past six months, our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia, and Nvidia" (PC Gamer quotes that sentence the same day). The Journal's first report, on Oct 30, had quoted the statement of December (the Journal's act of that day). The statement, as the image on its LinkedIn page shows it, says the reviews demonstrate "that we are a compliant and legitimate company"; CNN's profile of Alice Huang on Nov 10, which names no occasion, has it say it is a "compliant and legal company". A representative tells the Times, for its report of an inquiry, that the company is conducting an internal investigation into allegations of chip diversion and has repeatedly offered to cooperate with the U.S. government, and that those offers have gone unanswered. Bloomberg reports, in its account of a call by Nvidia's general counsel about the U.S. inquiry into the company, as the Business Times of Singapore carries it: it "has categorically denied the chip diversion allegations, and said that its outreach to the US government about the probe has gone unanswered", and it added that Singapore's investigation "into activities related to alleged chip diversion concluded earlier this year with no adverse action against Megaspeed". Bloomberg gives the response no day. Singapore's ministry says three days later that its investigations "into Megaspeed and six other individuals are ongoing" (its chip of Nov 12). CNBC Indonesia reports that Alice Huang's name "telah dihapus dari website perusahaan" (has been removed from the company's website). The report gives the removal no day and names no source for it
Declines to comment to the Times for its profile of Alice Huang. A commentator's newsletter of Nov 10 notes that its "public website identifies the facilities only as DC1 and DC2", their locations "described vaguely as" East South Asia. CNBC reports the next day, in a survey of its sites in Asia, that the three data centers listed on its website, "previously identified as being in Malaysia and Indonesia", are now described only as being in "East South Asia". Bloomberg had reported that change in December 2025 ("previously identified as being in Malaysia and Indonesia and now all listed as" East South Asia), so it is not a change of these days. No page gives it a day; the chip sits on the day of the first saved account in the fifteen days, and the pages describe what the site says, not where the data centers are
Says it takes U.S. export-control compliance "extremely seriously" and has cooperated with inspections. In a statement on its site: it "has retained a leading U.S. law firm to lead a comprehensive census of its graphics processing units (GPUs) and independently verify its export control compliance practices", and "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny"; it says it "stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority" and "is committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government". Channel NewsAsia reports that, in the comments under the statement it posted on LinkedIn on Nov 9, it replied "No" when asked "whether former executive Alice Huang was a spy". The report gives the reply no day
Taiwan's government
Its representative office in Washington tells the Journal it "doesn't comment on specific intelligence or security matters"
At the legislature its interior minister says "The national security authorities are actively investigating, and the Ministry of the Interior is cooperating" (Asia Economy, from a Taiwanese daily). Its premier declines to answer a question about Taiwan's part in the U.S. investigation; he says the government has records of her entries and exits and "would not say how many times she had visited" (Taiwan News). Its deputy foreign minister says she complied with entry rules and that the government is taking the necessary precautions, in Asia Economy's account of Nov 10; he declines to tell reporters under what status she entered, and adds that travellers who comply with the rules and have no criminal record in Taiwan would not face unnecessary restrictions (Taiwan News)
Its interior minister says, in the Journal's account of her words on Wednesday, that Alice Huang will be barred from returning to Taiwan and that security agencies are "continuing to investigate". Its interior minister says she entered Taiwan several times on a Hong Kong passport, is not in Taiwan now, and that her entry permit has been revoked; that had the authorities known she was a spy they would not have let her in; and, as the Central News Agency quotes her, "the police administration will provide full assistance" under the security laws (NTD). Taiwan News, that Wednesday afternoon in Taipei, has her tell lawmakers, by a Taiwanese daily's account, that "the government would review its screening procedures, including checks before entry, monitoring during visits, and penalties afterward". Before a committee meeting of the legislature on Wednesday, Nov 11 in Taipei, the head of its immigration agency tells reporters that government agencies have records of her visits, "including her entry and exit dates", and "declined to say whether she would be placed on a blacklist" (Taiwan News, in a page stamped 2:08 p.m. there, which is 1:08 a.m. Eastern; it does not give the hour of the exchange, and the chip sits on the local day its source names)
Its China-policy agency's spokesman, of a U.S. recommendation in 2024 to monitor her visits that the Times reported: "MAC has indeed never received such information"; the agency is not an intelligence agency, and "We are not sure whether other agencies received it"; without a lead, visitors get routine screening; it can neither confirm nor deny the allegations. The cabinet's spokesperson calls the case a cross-border cooperative investigation and declines to give details, citing the confidentiality of ongoing investigations; the immigration agency says it worked with security authorities to monitor her visits (Focus Taiwan). In the Central News Agency's Chinese-language account of the briefing after the cabinet meeting, the cabinet's spokesperson says that whether the case involves suspicion of a crime, and the investigative steps, are not public information for now; that an application by a Chinese national to visit on business sets off a joint review by the China-policy agency and the security agencies, with visits to those already admitted where intelligence calls for it; and that where espionage, or activity other than the permitted purpose, is verified, the entry permit is revoked at once and a national-security investigation opened. The immigration agency's official says there that her entry permit has been revoked and her entry barred. The head of its China-policy agency tells lawmakers she entered Taiwan three times in 2024 and five times in 2025, with no recorded visit this year, as a Hong Kong resident on business, and was not specially flagged during those visits (Focus Taiwan). In the Central News Agency's Chinese-language dispatch on the hearing, stamped 11:13 a.m. in Taipei on Nov 12 (10:13 p.m. Eastern on Nov 11; the chip sits on the local day, as its source names it), he adds that now that her identity is known she will be flagged and her entry controlled under the rule on residents of Hong Kong and Macau who may endanger national interests or public safety, that doubtful cases get a stricter review, and that applicants who raise security concerns are refused; asked about the U.S. media report that the United States had advised Taiwan in 2024 to monitor her visits, he answers that his agency did not know of this and that with important intelligence it would tighten entry screening. Its science minister, in Taiwan News: "an isolated incident" should have no real impact on Taiwan's AI development. The Journal reports, as To Vima carries the article, that Taiwanese authorities say they have revoked Alice Huang's entry permit and barred her from returning, and that officials say they "are now investigating whether her visits involved intelligence gathering or violated the island's anti-infiltration act"
Global Times newspaper in China
Writes: "Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows". ZeroHedge, relaying the commentary: "All it took were a few photographs showing Asian faces and Nvidia's previous efforts to push for relaxing trade curbs on China"; in its account the paper denies any government connection to the affair, says U.S. media are "going crazy", and warns that an "anti-China script" could disrupt technology and trade ties. In its own text the paper adds that even if the board opens an inquiry, "the investigation ought to stick to the facts and present solid evidence, rather than jumping to conclusions"
A commentary of Nov 10, "Jensen Huang Probe: Counterintelligence or Political Witch Hunt?", as the Seoul Economic Daily relays it: the reporting rests on anonymous sources and unverified material; "You cannot build next-generation graphics processing units on suspicion alone"
Writes of "Washington's increasingly hysterical anti-China climate", which it says "has fueled a new push for restrictions imposed in the name of national security, with the allegations surrounding Huang becoming fresh ammunition for what Chinese experts described as a witch hunt targeting people of Chinese descent"
Rep. Michael McCaul
Sen. Jim Banks
Sen. John Kennedy
A tie is a dated record, not a motive.
No document here shows that any tie prompted a report, a post or a statement. Each line ends at a person or a body, never at an act; the acts sit on the calendar at right.
13 of the 27 members drawn received an AnthroPAC contribution; 14 did not, and they pressed the matter too. The PAC paid 81 candidates in all, 38 Democrats and 43 Republicans. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom are themselves among the seven companies that agreed to buy Anthropic stock. Employees' gifts are their own money: 154 of the 535 sitting members received one from someone who gave Anthropic as employer, 19 of the 27 drawn here. The same count for Nvidia's employees is worded in each member's row. Ties the source article asserts but no document here supports are not drawn.
